one_line_idea: Signed-distance-field regression redistributes boundary-concentrated gradients across the whole image plane, and its benefit over per-pixel mask classification is predictable from how concentrated the mask-loss gradient field is (thin, elongated classes benefit; blob classes do not).
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Distance-transform-style regression targets are repeatedly rediscovered for thin-structure segmentation, but the community lacks a rule for when they help, and results across papers conflict.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Cross-entropy on masks concentrates useful gradient in a thin band around boundaries once interiors saturate, so classes whose gradient field has high spatial concentration (high Gini coefficient over pixels) train slowly; regressing a signed distance field spreads informative gradient over all pixels and helps exactly those classes, for optimization rather than representational reasons.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across Cityscapes classes, the SDF-vs-mask improvement in class IoU will correlate with the measured per-class gradient Gini coefficient at Spearman rho >= 0.6, with pole/fence/traffic-sign gaining at least 2 IoU and road/building within +-0.5 IoU. Kill the idea if rho < 0.3 or if blob classes gain as much as thin classes (uniform gain implies a different mechanism such as target smoothness).
why_important: It replaces a contradictory literature with a measurable predictor grounded in gradient allocation, and clarifies that the fix belongs to optimization (could be replicated by gradient reallocation) rather than to output representation per se.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Distance-map targets exist in many task papers; differentiating from the level-set-family supervision idea already in this window (W13-P1-B-080, which supervises all thresholds of a soft target), this idea makes a cross-class gradient-concentration law with a pre-registered correlation, which appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train DeepLabv3+ on Cityscapes with per-class binary mask heads vs per-class truncated SDF regression heads; log per-class per-pixel gradient concentration during training; correlate concentration with the per-class benefit.
main_risk: SDF targets require post-hoc thresholding whose tuning could contaminate the per-class comparison; a fixed, pre-registered thresholding rule is needed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Distance-target benefits are attributed to encoding shape priors, a representational story that predicts uniform gains rather than concentration-dependent gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Thin-class gains might come from the regression target's tolerance to sub-pixel boundary placement rather than gradient spreading, which the correlation design cannot fully separate without an extra gradient-reallocation arm.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ ResNet-50 (public, mmsegmentation) on Cityscapes (public) at 40k iterations, two arms x 2 seeds: about 2 days on one A100; gradient logging piggybacks on training.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: output target type (binary mask vs truncated signed distance field)
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: per-class IoU gains vs gradient-concentration statistics

one_line_idea: The Gaussian sigma of keypoint heatmap targets is an implicit learning-rate schedule, so annealing sigma during training should dominate any fixed sigma, and two runs ending at the same sigma but with different trajectories should end at measurably different accuracy.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Human-pose and keypoint pipelines encode targets as Gaussians with a hand-tuned sigma; the value is treated as a static representational choice and re-tuned per dataset and resolution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Target sigma controls the spatial support and magnitude of per-pixel gradients around each keypoint, so it functions as a spatial learning-rate and curriculum knob: large sigma early accelerates coarse localization, small sigma late sharpens precision, and the trajectory of sigma matters independently of its final value.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] A linear sigma anneal (from 3x to 1x the standard value) will beat the best fixed sigma by at least 0.5 AP on COCO keypoints, and two runs with identical final sigma but different anneal trajectories will differ by at least 0.3 AP. Kill the idea if the best fixed sigma matches all anneal schedules within 0.2 AP, which would mean sigma acts as a pure representational setting with no trajectory dependence.
why_important: Recasting a target-encoding hyperparameter as a schedule both removes a per-dataset tuning burden and provides the cleanest available demonstration that dense-target shape parameters have optimization-trajectory roles, a template applicable to soft edge widths and center-heatmap radii.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Sigma tuning studies exist, and coarse-to-fine heatmaps appear in some pipelines, but a controlled trajectory-vs-endpoint dissociation with pre-registered margins appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train HRNet-W32 on COCO keypoints with a sigma grid (fixed values) and three anneal trajectories sharing a final value; compare AP and PCK at matched budgets over 3 seeds.
main_risk: The standard OKS-based evaluation partially bakes in a scale tolerance that could mask precision differences produced by late-training small sigma.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Sigma is understood as a label-encoding smoothness constant whose best value is dataset-intrinsic, implying trajectory irrelevance.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Heatmap normalization and Adam may absorb most of the gradient-magnitude effects of sigma, leaving only the representational component that fixed tuning already captures.
fastest_falsification_experiment: HRNet-W32 (public weights/code) on COCO keypoints (public), 5 arms x 2 seeds at a 70-epoch reduced schedule: about 3 days on one A100; a cheaper MPII (public) version fits in 1 day.

one_line_idea: Classification-over-bins beats direct regression for dense continuous targets mainly because it bounds per-pixel gradient magnitude, so regression with matched per-pixel gradient clipping should erase most of the gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Discretize-then-classify target encodings (depth bins, quantized offsets) frequently outperform direct regression for dense prediction, and the standard explanation is that classification captures multimodality or richer supervision.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dominant active ingredient is gradient boundedness: cross-entropy over bins caps the per-pixel gradient regardless of error size, while L1/L2 regression lets outlier pixels dominate updates; on heavy-tailed targets this difference alone explains most of the gap, independent of any multimodality story.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Direct depth regression with per-pixel gradient clipping tuned to match the cross-entropy gradient-magnitude envelope will recover at least 60% of the (bin-classification minus plain-regression) delta1 gap on NYU Depth v2. Kill the idea if recovery is under 25%, or if bin classification retains its full advantage on a synthetic unimodal-target control where multimodality cannot be the explanation yet clipping-matched regression still loses.
why_important: Debunking the multimodality folklore in favor of a gradient-envelope mechanism tells practitioners they can keep simple regression heads (cheaper, no bin-design decisions) by fixing the optimizer side, and predicts exactly which target distributions need the fix.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Bins-vs-regression comparisons are common; the differentiation from this window's occupied idea W13-P1-B-024 (physical mixture fractions at boundaries) is explicit: this idea concerns gradient-envelope mechanics on arbitrary continuous targets, not physical mixing. The clipping-matched recovery design appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three arms on NYU Depth v2 (bins, plain L1, envelope-matched clipped L1) with matched backbones and schedules; log per-pixel gradient distributions to verify envelope matching; report delta1/AbsRel over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Adaptive bin methods entangle bin placement with encoding, so the comparison must use fixed uniform-in-log bins to isolate the envelope mechanism.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The community narrative credits distributional expressiveness (soft targets, multimodality) for bin-classification gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ordinal structure loss in naive bin classification should hurt, yet bins still win; if the win survives envelope matching, the real mechanism may be the softmax's implicit temperature adaptation, not boundedness.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ResNet-50 U-Net (torchvision, public) on NYU Depth v2 (public), 3 arms x 3 seeds, 8 epochs: about 1.5 days on one RTX 4090.

one_line_idea: Bounded offset parameterizations in dense detection heads win over absolute-coordinate regression not for representational reasons but because they compress the target range into the optimizer's stable step-size band, so an LR sweep should rescue absolute coordinates.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection heads regress normalized offsets relative to anchors, centers, or grid cells; folklore holds that absolute-coordinate regression is unlearnable, but the claim is almost never tested under matched tuning effort.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Offset parameterizations rescale the target distribution into a narrow numeric range, which co-adapts with default learning rates and initialization; absolute-coordinate failure is therefore primarily a step-size mismatch, and a proper LR/normalization sweep will close most of the gap on standard benchmarks.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] FCOS-style training with absolute pixel-coordinate targets plus a 6-point LR sweep and target standardization will come within 2.0 box AP of the offset baseline on COCO. Kill the idea if the best absolute arm remains more than 5 AP behind, which would indicate a genuine representational advantage of relative encoding (e.g., translation-equivariant targets matching convolutional structure).
why_important: If the gap is mostly tuning, target-encoding design space for dense localization opens up (e.g., global coordinates useful for tracking or association heads); if the gap survives, this is clean evidence that equivariance-aligned targets matter beyond optimization, sharpening a widely repeated but untested folklore.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Anchor-free papers ablate encodings under fixed LR; a tuning-matched adjudication between step-size and equivariance explanations appears missing. Distinct from occupied W13-P1-D-050 (mask-derived box targets), which changes supervision source, not coordinate parameterization.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train FCOS-ResNet-50 on COCO with (a) standard offsets, (b) absolute coordinates naive, (c) absolute standardized + LR sweep; report AP and per-scale AP over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Absolute targets break the fully convolutional weight-sharing assumption, so failure could reflect architecture-target mismatch rather than optimization, requiring a positional-encoding-augmented head as a control arm.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Relative offsets are considered obviously necessary, and absolute regression is dismissed without matched tuning.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Translation equivariance is a strong structural prior; no LR schedule can substitute for targets the shared filters cannot express, so the 5 AP kill bar may trigger.
fastest_falsification_experiment: FCOS-R50 (public, mmdetection) on COCO (public) at 1x schedule, 8 arms total: about 4 days on one A100, or 1.5 days using a COCO-minitrain subset (public split) for the sweep and full COCO only for the final two arms.

one_line_idea: Softmax versus per-class sigmoid output parameterization in semantic segmentation determines whether co-occurring classes exchange gradients competitively, predicting opposite confusion dynamics for class pairs that frequently share boundaries.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation heads use mutually exclusive softmax or independent per-class sigmoids somewhat interchangeably (sigmoids especially in multi-label and open-vocabulary settings), with the choice rarely analyzed as a training-dynamics variable.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Softmax couples class logits so that every positive update for class A at a pixel is a negative update for class B, creating zero-sum dynamics concentrated at co-occurring class pairs; sigmoid decouples them. Therefore softmax training should show anti-correlated within-run fluctuations of confusable-pair accuracies and faster separation of frequently adjacent classes, while sigmoid should show independent drift and more inter-class leakage at shared boundaries.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] For the top-5 co-occurring Cityscapes class pairs, the epoch-to-epoch correlation of per-class IoU fluctuations will be negative under softmax (mean r <= -0.3) and near zero under sigmoid (|r| <= 0.15), and sigmoid training will show at least 20% higher off-diagonal confusion mass restricted to adjacent-pair boundary bands. Kill the idea if fluctuation correlations do not differ by parameterization (gap < 0.15) or if confusion structure is identical within 5%.
why_important: It turns an arbitrary head-design choice into a predictable dynamics knob, with direct consequences for open-vocabulary and partially labeled settings where sigmoids are mandatory and the coupling loss must be replaced by something else.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Softmax-vs-sigmoid comparisons exist for final accuracy; the within-run anti-correlation signature and boundary-band confusion decomposition appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train SegFormer-B0 on Cityscapes with softmax and sigmoid heads, checkpoint every half epoch, compute per-class IoU trajectories and boundary-band confusion matrices, compare fluctuation correlation structure.
main_risk: Per-class IoU fluctuations are noisy at half-epoch resolution; distinguishing anti-correlation from evaluation noise needs many checkpoints and possibly multiple seeds, inflating cost moderately.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The head parameterization is considered an implementation detail that the loss and data dominate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Batch statistics and shared decoder features may couple classes far more strongly than the output nonlinearity does, drowning the softmax-specific zero-sum signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 (public, mmsegmentation) on Cityscapes (public), 2 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations with dense checkpointing: about 2 days on one A100.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: within-run per-class IoU fluctuation correlations + boundary-band confusion

one_line_idea: Dice loss is an implicit instance-size reweighting schedule whose strength grows as predictions sharpen, predicting that dice beats cross-entropy only when the target size distribution is heavy-tailed beyond a measurable threshold.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dice and cross-entropy dominate segmentation training and their relative merits are folklore (dice for imbalance, CE for stability), but no quantitative rule tells a practitioner which to use on a given dataset.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dice normalizes each structure's contribution by its predicted+true size, so per-pixel gradients scale inversely with structure size, and this reweighting intensifies during training as soft predictions contract toward the structure; dice-vs-CE outcomes are therefore governed by the tail exponent of the size distribution, not by class imbalance per se.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across datasets and resampled variants engineered to vary the structure-size tail (subsampling large instances), the dice-minus-CE gap will flip sign at a consistent tail statistic (within a factor of 2 across datasets), and time-resolved per-size gradient shares will show dice's small-structure share growing by at least 2x over training. one_line_idea: Structured surrogate losses like Lovász hinge help exactly when a model's errors are spatially clustered, because their pixel-gradient coupling coordinates updates within an error blob, predicting the gain from a pre-training error-autocorrelation measurement.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Lovász-softmax and similar IoU surrogates beat cross-entropy in some segmentation setups and not others, and the community has no account of which setups benefit.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] These losses couple gradients across pixels of the same class within an image (through the sorted-error construction), effectively making coordinated blob-level corrections; when errors are spatially independent the coupling adds variance without benefit, so the spatial autocorrelation length of the error field determines the sign of the effect.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 8 model-dataset configurations, the Lovász-minus-CE mIoU gap will correlate with pre-measured error autocorrelation length at Spearman rho >= 0.6, and configurations with autocorrelation below 4 pixels will show gaps within +-0.3 mIoU. Kill the idea if rho < 0.25 or if spatially-shuffled-error controls (patch-permuted training images) preserve the Lovász advantage, which would locate the mechanism elsewhere.
why_important: It converts an unreliable loss-choice folklore into a cheap pre-measurement rule and identifies gradient coupling, not metric alignment, as the operative property of structured surrogates.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Lovász losses are motivated as IoU surrogates (metric alignment); the error-autocorrelation moderator and the coupling mechanism appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take 8 public segmentation configs spanning CNN/transformer and two datasets; measure baseline error autocorrelation; retrain each with Lovász; correlate gap with autocorrelation; add one patch-permuted control.
main_risk: Error autocorrelation and dataset identity are confounded; the resampled and permuted controls are essential to break the confound, adding arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Structured surrogates are believed to help because they optimize the evaluation metric more directly, implying dataset-independent gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The sorted-error construction also changes the effective example weighting (hardest pixels dominate), which is an OHEM-like mechanism that could explain gains without any spatial-coupling story.

one_line_idea: Focal loss is functionally an annealed hard-pixel selection schedule: replacing it with explicit top-k pixel selection whose k follows focal's shrinking effective-support trajectory should reproduce its gains, killing the reweighting-form story.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Focal loss is the default for dense detection and many segmentation setups, credited to its specific polynomial down-weighting form; countless variants tweak the form.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] What matters is not the weighting form but the induced trajectory of effective support: as the model improves, the fraction of pixels with non-negligible focal gradient shrinks, making focal an automatic anneal from all-pixel to hard-pixel training; any selection scheme matching that support trajectory will match focal.

Kill the idea if trajectory-matched top-k lags focal by more than 1.0 AP, which would mean the soft weighting form carries independent value.
why_important: A positive result collapses the focal-variant cottage industry into a single scheduling principle and gives a knob (support trajectory) that can be designed directly instead of through loss-form tinkering.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Focal-vs-OHEM comparisons exist at fixed settings; matching the measured support trajectory as the equivalence variable appears new.

community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The focal form itself (the gamma exponent) is treated as the innovation, as evidenced by the many form-variant papers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hard selection introduces gradient discontinuities at the k-th boundary that soft weighting avoids, which could destabilize training in ways trajectory matching cannot fix.

why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense heads share features across pixels, so per-pixel implicit decay may wash out at the shared-feature level where the schedule actually operates.

one_line_idea: Boundary-region learning is gradient-starved until interiors saturate, making interior-then-boundary acquisition an optimization-forced order; boundary emphasis should therefore only matter under short training budgets, with a predictable crossover.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Numerous papers report gains from emphasizing boundary regions in segmentation losses, while others find no benefit, and long-schedule reproductions often shrink the gains; the field lacks a governing account.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Early in training, interior pixels dominate the gradient budget because they are numerous and initially wrong; boundary pixels receive meaningful gradient only after interiors saturate. Boundary emphasis merely pulls this phase forward, so its value decays with budget and vanishes when the natural boundary phase completes within the schedule.

Kill the idea if boundary emphasis keeps helping by >= 1.5 points at 2x the standard budget, which would falsify the phase-completion account in favor of a permanent optimization barrier at boundaries.
why_important: It explains contradictory boundary-loss literature with a single budget-dependent law, tells practitioners when boundary emphasis is worth it, and reframes acquisition order as gradient-budget allocation that schedules can manipulate.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Boundary losses are abundant; the budget-crossover law and the interior-saturation timing prediction appear untested. This idea deliberately makes no claim about labeling practices; it is purely an optimization-dynamics account.

main_risk: Boundary metrics are sensitive to the band width definition; pre-registering band widths (4 and 8 px) avoids post-hoc metric shopping.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boundary emphasis is viewed as adding information the plain loss lacks, implying budget-independent gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary pixels may be starved by irreducible ambiguity rather than gradient competition, in which case no budget extension completes the phase and the 2x-budget arm will keep showing gains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (mmsegmentation, public) on Cityscapes (public), 4 budgets x 2 arms x 2 seeds: about 3.5 days on one A100 (short budgets dominate the grid cheaply).

one_line_idea: Class-frequency loss reweighting interacts destructively with momentum: rare-class gradient bursts get smeared into subsequent unrelated batches, so reweighting gains should shrink as momentum grows, an interaction nobody tunes for.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Inverse-frequency loss weighting is a default remedy for class imbalance in segmentation, and momentum 0.9 is a default optimizer setting; they are tuned independently in every codebase.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Rare classes appear in occasional bursts; amplifying their loss creates large transient gradients that momentum carries into many following steps where the rare class is absent, applying stale rare-class updates against unrelated batches and partially undoing the intended effect; lower momentum or momentum-reset-on-burst should restore the reweighting benefit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The rare-class IoU benefit of 10x reweighting will be at least 2x larger at momentum 0.5 than at momentum 0.99 on Cityscapes rare classes, and per-step interference (cosine between the momentum buffer and current batch gradient after rare bursts) will be significantly more negative under high momentum (mean cosine <= -0.05 vs >= -0.01). Kill the idea if the reweighting benefit is momentum-independent within 20% or if the interference cosine shows no burst-conditioned structure.
why_important: This is distinct from the occupied finding W13-P1-D-031 (reweighting as disguised score recalibration): here the claim is a mechanistic optimizer interaction that predicts WHEN reweighting works at all, with a cheap fix (burst-conditioned momentum handling) if confirmed.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Loss reweighting and momentum are both ancient, but their interaction through burst timing appears unmeasured in dense prediction.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid over momentum {0.5, 0.9, 0.99} x reweighting {1x, 10x} on Cityscapes with DeepLabv3+, log momentum-buffer/batch-gradient cosines around rare-class bursts, compare rare-class IoU deltas.
main_risk: Adam's per-parameter normalization complicates the story relative to SGD+momentum; running SGD first isolates the mechanism, with an Adam arm as generalization check.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Reweighting strength and momentum are treated as orthogonal hyperparameters with no interaction worth reporting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Momentum smearing may actually help rare classes by extending their effective presence across steps (a mild replay), making the interaction positive rather than destructive.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 6 arms x 2 seeds at 20k iterations with SGD: about 2 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Whether combining two dense losses helps is determined by the spatial structure of their per-pixel gradient disagreement: structured disagreement (different losses own different pixel populations) yields complementary gains, diffuse disagreement yields averaging.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Compound losses (e.g., CE+dice) are ubiquitous defaults in dense prediction, yet combination outcomes vary by task and no principle distinguishes complementary pairs from redundant or conflicting ones.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Two losses help jointly when their per-pixel gradient sign disagreements concentrate on distinct, coherent pixel populations (e.g., one loss dominates boundaries, the other interiors), so each population gets a consistent signal; when disagreement is spatially diffuse the combination merely averages and adds variance.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 10 loss pairs on two segmentation datasets, a disagreement-structure index (mutual information between disagreement indicator and pixel-population labels) will separate pairs whose combination beats both singles from pairs that do not, with AUC >= 0.8. why_important: A validated structure test would let practitioners screen loss combinations with a half-epoch measurement instead of full factorial training, and would explain why the same compound loss helps on one dataset and not another.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-conflict analyses exist for multi-task learning across tasks; applying population-structured conflict analysis to same-task loss combination appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 10 documented loss pairs, measure disagreement structure on a half-epoch probe run, then train all singles and combinations to convergence and test whether the index predicts synergy sign.
main_risk: Defining pixel populations (boundary bands, size classes, frequency bands) involves choices; pre-registering three population partitions and requiring consistency guards against index shopping.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Compound losses are assumed beneficial by default (belt and suspenders), with failures attributed to weighting rather than structural redundancy.

one_line_idea: Temperature in pixel-level contrastive objectives sets the effective number of negatives that receive gradient, and the right temperature is determined by the intra-class visual diversity of the dataset, predicting opposite tuning directions for homogeneous versus diverse datasets.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Low temperature concentrates gradient on the hardest negatives; in dense settings the hardest negatives for diverse classes are frequently semantically same-class pixels (other instances, distant parts), so low temperature actively teaches wrong invariances on diverse datasets while sharpening useful boundaries on homogeneous ones; the optimal temperature therefore increases with measured intra-class feature diversity.

one_line_idea: Constant-LR-plus-EMA matches decayed schedules on interior-dominated metrics but systematically lags on boundary-sensitive metrics, because weight averaging only mimics decay where the local loss is quadratic, which boundary directions violate.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] A schedule-free training current (constant LR with strong EMA or iterate averaging) claims parity with decayed schedules, validated mostly on classification and mean metrics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Averaging iterates equals decaying LR only under local quadratic structure; dense boundary directions have non-quadratic, asymmetric loss geometry (small shifts asymmetrically flip pixel sets), so the averaged weights land measurably off the low-LR limit specifically in boundary behavior while matching in interiors, producing a metric-dependent verdict on schedule-free training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Constant-LR+EMA will match a matched-budget cosine run within 0.2 mIoU overall on Cityscapes but lose at least 1.0 point on 4px-trimap boundary accuracy, and the deficit will shrink monotonically as the constant LR is lowered (approaching quadratic validity). Kill the idea if boundary parity holds within 0.3 points at standard constant LR, which would certify schedule-free training for boundary-critical dense use.
why_important: Schedule-free methods are being adopted for convenience; knowing they carry a boundary-specific tax (or certifying they do not) matters for dense deployments and pins down where the quadratic-equivalence argument actually holds in real networks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Averaging-equals-decay arguments and schedule-free optimizers are current topics; the spatially-resolved validity test on dense tasks appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train Cityscapes DeepLabv3+ under matched budgets: cosine decay vs constant+EMA at 3 constant-LR levels; evaluate mean and trimap metrics; verify the LR-dependence of the boundary deficit.
main_risk: EMA decay constant and the constant-LR level jointly determine the effective averaging window; a small grid over both is needed to avoid strawmanning the schedule-free arm.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Averaging-based schedule-free training is presented as a drop-in replacement for decay, with parity claims implicitly metric-uniform.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary directions may be effectively quadratic at the relevant noise scale, or EMA's implicit window may adapt adequately, producing full spatial parity.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 5 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 2.5 days on one A100; trimap evaluation is post-hoc.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: decayed schedule vs constant-LR+EMA at varying LR

one_line_idea: Strong-augmentation-early, weak-late ordering beats the reverse only under short budgets, because high-LR phases absorb high-variance augmentation gradients while low-LR phases cannot, predicting an ordering-by-budget interaction with a crossover.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Augmentation curricula are scheduled by intuition, with most recipes ramping augmentation up or holding it constant, and some (detection endgame) turning it off late; there is no accepted law for ordering augmentation strength against the LR schedule.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Augmentation adds gradient variance that is cheap to absorb when LR-driven noise already dominates (early, high LR) and expensive when the model is consolidating (late, low LR); therefore strong-early/weak-late dominates the reverse ordering, but the margin shrinks as total budget grows because both orderings eventually see enough clean low-LR steps.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At a 25% budget on Cityscapes, strong-early ordering will beat strong-late by at least 1.0 mIoU; at full budget the gap will shrink below 0.3 mIoU, with the crossover budget identifiable within a factor of 2 across two architectures. Kill the idea if strong-late wins at short budgets, or if the gap does not shrink with budget (ordering matters asymptotically, implying a basin-selection rather than noise-absorption mechanism).
why_important: It gives augmentation scheduling a falsifiable design rule tied to the LR schedule and budget, unifying the endgame augmentation-off trick and curriculum intuitions under one noise-absorption account.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Augmentation curricula exist in scattered recipes; the LR-phase noise-absorption law with a budget crossover appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Cross {strong-early, constant, strong-late} x budgets {25%, 50%, 100%} x 2 architectures on Cityscapes with matched total augmentation exposure; compare mIoU and late-phase gradient variance.
main_risk: Matching total augmentation exposure across orderings requires care (equal integrals of strength over steps), else exposure, not ordering, drives the result.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Augmentation strength ordering is treated as a free design choice or ramped up to stabilize early training, the opposite of the noise-absorption prescription.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Early strong augmentation may prevent formation of clean low-level features that later phases cannot recover (a critical-period effect), reversing the predicted ordering at short budgets.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 9 arms x 2 seeds mostly at reduced budgets: about 3.5 days on one A100.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: mIoU ordering gaps vs budget with crossover localization

one_line_idea: The linear-probe-then-finetune advantage for dense tasks can be earned adaptively: hold the backbone until the head's gradient norm falls below a fixed fraction of the backbone's, then release, matching tuned two-stage recipes without tuning the stage boundary.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Two-stage fine-tuning (train head first, then everything) is known to protect pretrained features, but the stage boundary is a tuned hyperparameter that practitioners set by convention (fixed epochs).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The damage two-stage training prevents is caused by large random-head gradients flowing into the backbone; the natural stage boundary is therefore when the head-to-backbone gradient-norm ratio drops below a small constant, and an online rule releasing the backbone at that crossing captures the full benefit across setups with one universal constant.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The gradient-ratio release rule with a single constant (tuned once on one setup) will come within 0.3 mIoU/AbsRel-equivalent of the best fixed-boundary two-stage recipe on 4 held-out dense setups, while the best single-stage baseline trails by at least 0.8 on at least 2 of them. Kill the idea if the universal constant fails to transfer (worse than single-stage on any setup) or per-setup re-tuning of the constant is required to reach parity.
why_important: It removes a tuned stage boundary from a widespread recipe, tests the interface-damage account of two-stage training's benefit, and produces an online diagnostic that generalizes to any new-head-on-pretrained-trunk situation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Two-stage protection is established folklore; an online gradient-ratio release criterion with a transferability claim appears untested for dense tasks.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 5 dense fine-tuning setups (2 seg, 1 depth, 1 det, 1 keypoint), tune the ratio constant on setup 1, apply frozen to the rest, compare against fixed-boundary grids and single-stage baselines over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Gradient norms depend on loss scale and head architecture, so the ratio must be normalized per-parameter to have any chance of transferring as a single constant.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The stage boundary is a per-task hyperparameter without a governing online signal.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Backbone damage may depend on gradient direction (conflict with pretrained structure), not magnitude, in which case the norm-ratio rule triggers at the wrong times.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0/ADE20K, DeepLabv3+/VOC, DPT/NYUv2, RetinaNet/COCO-minitrain, HRNet/MPII (all public), ratio rule vs grids at short schedules: about 4 days on one A100; the 2-setup core (1.5 days) gives an early read.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: backbone release criterion (online gradient ratio vs fixed boundary)
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: transfer parity across setups with one constant

one_line_idea: Dense fine-tuning proceeds in two intrinsic phases, normalization/bias adaptation first and weight-matrix rotation second, and the first phase alone accounts for most in-domain gain, making the phase boundary a natural budget knob.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Parameter-movement analyses in fine-tuning show norm/bias parameters move disproportionately, and bias/norm-only tuning is a known cheap baseline, but when and why full-weight movement becomes necessary in dense transfer is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Early fine-tuning gains come from re-centering activation statistics (norm/bias), which requires no feature rewriting; weight matrices begin rotating substantially only after this re-centering saturates, and the second phase contributes mainly on classes/structures absent from pretraining, so the phase decomposition predicts which tasks can stop after phase one.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Time-resolved parameter-movement decomposition on ADE20K fine-tuning will show norm/bias movement leading weight rotation by at least 3x in normalized units over the first 20% of steps, and freezing weights after the measured phase-one saturation will retain at least 80% of full fine-tuning's mIoU gain on pretraining-adjacent classes but under 50% on pretraining-distant classes. Kill the idea if movement is phase-mixed from the start (lead < 1.5x) or the retained-gain split does not follow pretraining adjacency.
why_important: It gives fine-tuning a mechanistic timeline that explains when cheap adaptation suffices, connects parameter-movement observations to a testable two-phase law, and provides a measurable stopping signal (phase-one saturation) rather than a budget guess.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Bias/norm-tuning baselines are known; the temporal phase structure and adjacency-split prediction for dense transfer appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune DINOv2-based segmentation on ADE20K logging per-parameter-group movement; identify phase-one saturation; run freeze-after-phase-one arms; split evaluation by class adjacency to pretraining data proxies.
main_risk: Defining pretraining adjacency requires a proxy (e.g., zero-shot probe accuracy per class before fine-tuning), which must be pre-registered to avoid circularity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Fine-tuning is viewed as a homogeneous process where all parameters co-adapt continuously.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimizer normalization (Adam) can equalize apparent movement scales, and the phase structure may be an artifact of LR warmup rather than intrinsic adaptation ordering.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DINOv2 ViT-S + linear/UperNet head (public) on ADE20K (public), instrumented fine-tuning + 3 freeze-point arms x 2 seeds: about 3 days on one A100.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: freeze timing relative to measured phase boundary

one_line_idea: Forgetting of pretraining abilities during dense fine-tuning is episodic rather than gradual, concentrated in identifiable step windows tied to LR milestones and batch composition, so cheap interventions targeted at those windows should preserve abilities at negligible cost.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fine-tuning for a dense task degrades the backbone's general abilities (retrieval, classification probes), and mitigation is usually continuous (regularization toward init) with a constant cost throughout training.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Ability loss is not a smooth drift: probe accuracy on pretraining-proxy tasks drops in discrete episodes coinciding with LR increases/milestones and rare-content batches, because forgetting requires large coordinated updates that only those windows provide; guarding only those windows (temporary trust-region or EMA fallback) preserves abilities nearly as well as continuous regularization at a fraction of the interference.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] With probes evaluated every 200 steps during ADE20K fine-tuning of a DINOv2 backbone, at least 60% of total probe-accuracy loss will occur within windows covering under 15% of steps, the windows will replicate across seeds (Jaccard >= 0.5), and window-targeted guarding will retain within 20% of the ability preservation of continuous L2-to-init at under half the dense-task accuracy cost. Kill the idea if loss is quasi-uniform (top 15% of windows hold < 30% of loss) or windows are seed-idiosyncratic (Jaccard < 0.2).
why_important: Episodic forgetting changes mitigation design from constant-pressure regularization to event-triggered protection, and the window statistics expose which training events actually destroy pretrained structure in dense adaptation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Forgetting curves are usually plotted per epoch, hiding step-level structure; the episodicity claim and window-targeted mitigation appear untested for dense fine-tuning.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument fine-tuning with frequent frozen-feature probes (ImageNet-100 linear probe as proxy ability), detect drop episodes, correlate with LR events and batch statistics, then compare window-guarding vs continuous regularization arms.
main_risk: Frequent probing is expensive; using cached probe heads on frozen feature snapshots every 200 steps keeps cost manageable but limits probe suite breadth.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Forgetting is modeled as gradual interference accumulating smoothly with steps, motivating always-on regularizers.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Episodes may be artifacts of probe noise at high checkpoint frequency; the seed-replication requirement is designed to catch this, and failure there kills the idea honestly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DINOv2 ViT-S (public) fine-tuned on ADE20K (public) with ImageNet-100 (public) probes, instrumented run + 2 mitigation arms x 2 seeds: about 3.5 days on one A100.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: step-resolved probing + window-targeted vs continuous protection

one_line_idea: Head initialization scale bifurcates dense fine-tuning into feature-reuse and feature-rewrite regimes at a sharp threshold, making one init hyperparameter a regime selector that explains bimodal fine-tuning outcomes.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense heads are initialized by generic schemes with an arbitrary gain factor; fine-tuning outcomes on similar setups are anecdotally bimodal (sometimes preserving pretrained behavior, sometimes rebuilding features) without a recognized controlling variable.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Small-gain heads produce small early gradients, keeping the backbone near its pretrained function (lazy/reuse regime); large-gain heads inject gradients that push the backbone out of the pretrained basin within the first hundreds of steps (rich/rewrite regime); the transition is sharp in init gain and its location is roughly predictable from first-step gradient-norm ratios.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Sweeping head init gain over two orders of magnitude on two dense setups will yield bimodal final backbone drift (CKA to init clustering into two groups separated by at least 0.2 CKA), with the transition confined to under half an order of magnitude in gain, and first-100-step gradient-ratio measurements will locate the threshold within a factor of 2. Kill the idea if drift varies smoothly (unimodal spread) across the sweep or the transition spans more than one order of magnitude.
why_important: A regime selector hiding in an ignored init constant would explain fine-tuning irreproducibility across codebases (different default gains), and give deliberate control over reuse-vs-rewrite, which matters when pretraining abilities must be preserved.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Lazy-vs-rich training regimes are studied theoretically for width/scale; head-init gain as the practical regime knob in dense transfer appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Init-gain sweeps on SegFormer/ADE20K and DPT/NYUv2 with fixed LR; measure final backbone CKA drift, dense accuracy, and pretraining-probe retention per gain; test threshold sharpness and its gradient-ratio predictability.
main_risk: LR and init gain trade off; a two-dimensional (gain x LR) mini-grid is needed to show the bifurcation is not just an effective-LR artifact, roughly doubling cost.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Head init is considered a numerical nicety with no qualitative effect once warmup exists.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Warmup plus Adam normalization may compress the effective early step sizes so strongly that all gains land in one regime, flattening the bifurcation in practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 (public) on ADE20K and DPT (public) on NYU Depth v2, 8 gains x 2 setups x 1 seed + boundary replication at short schedules: about 3.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: The weight-update matrices of full dense-task fine-tuning have systematically higher effective rank than classification fine-tuning on matched backbones, quantifying why low-rank adaptation recipes ported from classification underfit dense tasks.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Low-rank adaptation settings (rank, placement) are ported from language/classification recipes to dense vision tasks, and dense practitioners anecdotally report needing higher ranks, without a measurement of what rank the task intrinsically demands.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The intrinsic dimensionality of the required weight change is a task property: dense prediction requires spatially diverse feature edits (many independent directions across scales and positions), so the effective rank (participation ratio of singular values) of full fine-tuning deltas will be several-fold higher for dense tasks than classification on the same backbone, concentrated in spatial-mixing layers.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a fixed ViT-B backbone, the median effective rank of attention/MLP weight deltas after full fine-tuning will be at least 3x higher for ADE20K segmentation than for ImageNet-100 classification at matched accuracy saturation, with the largest ratios in spatial-mixing (attention) layers, and truncating dense deltas to classification-typical ranks will lose at least 2 mIoU. Kill the idea if the rank ratio is under 1.5x or truncation to low rank costs under 0.5 mIoU (dense edits are low-rank after all).
why_important: It grounds adapter-rank selection in a measurable task property instead of ported folklore, predicts which layers need capacity, and characterizes dense transfer as intrinsically higher-dimensional, a claim with consequences for parameter-efficient method design generally.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Intrinsic-dimension measurements exist for language fine-tuning; a controlled dense-vs-classification rank comparison on matched vision backbones appears missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Full fine-tune ViT-B (MAE or DINOv2 init) on ADE20K and ImageNet-100; compute per-layer delta effective ranks; run delta-truncation arms at several ranks; compare accuracy loss curves per task.
main_risk: Effective rank depends on training length and LR (deltas keep growing); matching tasks at accuracy-saturation checkpoints rather than fixed steps is essential and must be pre-registered.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Fine-tuning updates are assumed low-rank in general, with dense tasks expected to comply with the same adapter recipes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High measured rank may reflect optimizer noise accumulation rather than functionally necessary directions; the truncation arms directly test functional necessity and protect against this artifact.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ViT-B MAE (public) fine-tuned on ADE20K (public, UperNet head) and ImageNet-100 (public), plus truncation evaluation: about 4 days on one A100; SVD analysis is post-hoc on saved deltas.

one_line_idea: Dense fine-tuning exits the linearly-connected basin of its initialization within a few hundred steps while classification fine-tuning stays connected for most of training, giving a sharp geometric signature of how much dense adaptation restructures solutions.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Linear mode connectivity (no loss barrier on the straight path between two weight vectors) is a standard probe of whether training stayed in one basin, used mainly in classification studies; dense fine-tuning's basin behavior is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense objectives reshape spatial-mixing computations enough that the fine-tuned solution leaves the init-connected basin early, whereas classification fine-tuning famously stays connected; the exit time (first step whose interpolation to init shows a barrier) is therefore a task-complexity signature, earlier for dense tasks and earlier still for structurally novel target types.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Interpolation barriers (loss increase at midpoint exceeding 10% of endpoint loss) will appear within the first 5% of steps for ADE20K segmentation fine-tuning but not until after 50% of steps (if at all) for ImageNet-100 classification fine-tuning on the same DINOv2 backbone, replicated over 3 seeds. Kill the idea if dense fine-tuning stays barrier-free past 25% of steps or classification exits as early as dense (no task separation).
why_important: Basin-exit timing gives a concrete, cheap geometry probe for how invasive a fine-tuning task is, with practical consequences (checkpoint averaging and model-merging methods assume connectivity, and this law predicts exactly when they break for dense models).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Connectivity studies concentrate on classification and pretraining; time-resolved basin-exit comparison across task types on matched backbones appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fine-tune both tasks from the same init, saving dense checkpoints; compute init-to-checkpoint interpolation loss curves on task loss; locate first-barrier steps; verify with 3 seeds and one alternative barrier definition.
main_risk: Barrier measurements need matched normalization statistics along the path (BN/LN buffers interpolated consistently), a known pitfall that must be handled explicitly.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Fine-tuning is assumed to stay near init (motivating merging/averaging practices) regardless of task type.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Apparent barriers may reflect head-parameter mismatch rather than backbone basin exit; measuring barriers with per-checkpoint re-fitted heads isolates the backbone claim.

one_line_idea: Intermediate-task fine-tuning helps dense targets mostly by delivering a well-conditioned head and normalization state rather than better features, so transplanting only those components from the intermediate model should reproduce most of the stepping-stone gain.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fine-tuning through an intermediate task (e.g., generic segmentation before a specialized dense task) often beats direct transfer, and the benefit is attributed to representation enrichment.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] For dense targets, much of the stepping-stone benefit is optimization-mechanical: the intermediate stage leaves behind an adapted head geometry and normalization statistics that condition the final fine-tune (no random-head shock, statistics already in-range), so transplanting head+norm parameters onto the ORIGINAL backbone recovers most of the gain without any intermediate-feature content.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 3 intermediate-to-target dense pipelines, transplanting only head and normalization parameters (backbone reset to original pretrained weights) will recover at least 50% of the full stepping-stone gain, and the residual will correlate with target-class distance from the intermediate task. Kill the idea if head+norm transplant recovers under 20% of the gain in all pipelines, which would confirm the representational account and kill the mechanical one.
why_important: If conditioning, not content, drives stepping stones, practitioners can skip expensive intermediate fine-tunes by initializing heads/norms cheaply (few-epoch head-only training), and the community narrative about representation enrichment gets a needed audit.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Intermediate-task transfer is studied at the level of task pairs and gains; the component-transplant decomposition (head+norm vs backbone content) appears untested for dense pipelines.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Three pipelines (e.g., COCO-seg to VOC-seg, ADE20K to Cityscapes, COCO-det to pedestrian subset): full stepping stone vs head+norm transplant vs direct transfer, 2 seeds each, matched final-stage budgets.
main_risk: Head transplant requires matching class spaces or an alignment layer; pipelines must be chosen where the head structure is target-compatible, limiting generality of the test set.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stepping-stone gains are read as evidence that the intermediate task teaches transferable features.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Representational enrichment may genuinely dominate for distant targets, and the transplant may even hurt by importing intermediate-task biases into the head, driving recovery below the kill bar.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) pipelines over COCO/VOC/Cityscapes/ADE20K (all public) at short final-stage schedules, 9 arms total: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: The depth of the early-fine-tuning accuracy dip carries no information about final dense-task quality, debunking the practice of culling fine-tuning runs by their first-epochs behavior.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Fine-tuning runs commonly show an early transient dip (the pretrained function is disturbed before task adaptation wins); practitioners and automated sweep tools often terminate runs early based on early-phase metrics.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The dip depth is governed by interface variables (head init, warmup, first-batch composition) that are nearly independent of the variables governing final quality (data fit, capacity, schedule tail), so early-dip-based run selection is close to random selection and silently discards good configurations.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 40 fine-tuning configurations spanning LR, head init, warmup, and schedule on two dense setups, the rank correlation between dip depth (worst validation metric in the first 5% of steps) and final accuracy will satisfy |rho| < 0.25, and early-termination of the worst-dip half would discard at least 35% of the top-quartile final performers. Kill the idea if |rho| >= 0.45, in which case dip depth is a legitimate selection signal and the folklore stands.
why_important: Sweep budgets increasingly use early stopping of runs; if the early dip is uninformative for dense fine-tuning, current practice systematically biases hyperparameter search toward smooth-starting but mediocre configurations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Early-phase run-selection heuristics are studied for training-from-scratch classification; their validity for the dense fine-tuning transient appears unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run the 40-config sweep to completion on both setups, record full trajectories, compute dip-final correlations and the counterfactual loss of dip-based culling policies at several culling fractions.
main_risk: The result depends on the config distribution sampled; pre-registering the sweep space to mirror common practice (published recipe ranges) keeps the conclusion relevant rather than artificially constructed.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A run that starts badly is assumed to end badly, justifying early culling in sweep tooling defaults.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Extreme dips may genuinely flag divergence-adjacent configurations, creating a real correlation concentrated in the tail that the global rank statistic would detect and count against the debunk.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0/ADE20K and DPT/NYUv2 (public), 40 configs x 2 setups at short schedules (full trajectories logged): about 5 days on one A100; a 20-config pilot (2.5 days) gives a preliminary verdict.

one_line_idea: The folklore 10x head-LR multiplier is a proxy for equalizing head and backbone adaptation timescales, so the optimal multiplier should collapse toward 1 as head initialization quality improves, unifying two separate fine-tuning rituals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense fine-tuning recipes assign the new head a 10x higher LR than the backbone, a constant inherited across a decade of codebases and never derived.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The multiplier compensates for the head starting at random while the backbone starts converged: it approximately equalizes the two modules' time-to-adaptation. If the head is pre-adapted (probe-initialized), the compensation is unnecessary, so the optimal multiplier is a decreasing function of head-init quality, approaching 1 for fully probed heads; the 10x constant is thus a special case of one underlying variable (initial adaptation asymmetry).

Kill the idea if the optimal multiplier is independent of init quality (same optimum within noise across columns), which would leave the 10x constant unexplained by adaptation asymmetry.
why_important: It merges two rituals (head-LR multipliers and head pre-training) into one variable, letting practitioners trade them off deliberately, and demonstrates on a concrete constant how recipe folklore encodes hidden state variables.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both rituals are ubiquitous; the interaction experiment that unifies them appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: The 4x3 grid on SegFormer/ADE20K and RetinaNet/COCO-minitrain over 2 seeds, with head-init quality controlled by probe-training length; report the optimum shift and interaction.
main_risk: Probed heads change more than adaptation asymmetry (they also change early gradient direction quality); measuring first-epoch head movement verifies the intended manipulation.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The 10x multiplier is treated as a task-intrinsic constant of dense transfer rather than a function of init state.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Head LR may mainly control late-phase head expressiveness rather than early adaptation, in which case the optimum would track schedule length, not init quality.

one_line_idea: Re-initializing the final backbone block before dense fine-tuning helps precisely when the pretraining objective's terminal computations conflict with dense decoding, a conflict measurable as high initial gradient opposition in that block.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Surgical re-initialization of late layers before fine-tuning is a known trick with inconsistent results across setups, applied by trial and error.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Late pretrained blocks encode objective-specific terminal computations (e.g., global pooling preparation) that dense decoding must actively undo; when the angle between early fine-tuning gradients and the pretrained block's function is strongly opposed, resetting the block removes an obstacle, while for aligned setups resetting destroys useful structure. The measured initial gradient-opposition score in the final block therefore predicts the sign of the reset effect.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 8 (pretraining, dense-task) combinations, the sign of the reset effect (reset minus no-reset final accuracy) will agree with the sign predicted by the initial opposition score in at least 7 of 8 cases, with effect magnitudes exceeding 0.5 mIoU/AP in at least 4 cases. Kill the idea if agreement is at chance (4-5 of 8) or all effects are under 0.3 (reset is inert in modern recipes and the folklore is vestigial).
why_important: It converts an unreliable trick into a decision rule with a one-batch diagnostic, and maps which pretraining objectives leave dense-hostile terminal structure, informing pretraining design for dense consumers.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Layer-reset studies exist for classification transfer; the gradient-opposition predictor and dense-task focus appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid {4 pretrained inits: supervised, contrastive-style, masked-image, self-distilled} x {2 dense tasks: ADE20K seg, NYUv2 depth}, each with reset/no-reset arms; compute opposition scores from one pre-training-free batch; compare predicted vs realized effect signs.
main_risk: The opposition score definition (cosine between block gradient and a function-preservation direction) has freedom; pre-registering one definition and one backup avoids diagnostic shopping.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Late-layer resetting is viewed as generic regularization (fresh capacity) rather than removal of objective-specific conflicting structure.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reset effects may be dominated by changed effective LR in the reset block (fresh weights train faster), a mechanism independent of any conflict, which the opposition score would fail to track.

one_line_idea: Frequency-resolved error curves of dense predictors collapse onto one universal acquisition trajectory when time is reparameterized by integrated learning rate, making spectral acquisition order a schedule-invariant law rather than an architecture story.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Networks fit low spatial frequencies before high ones, and dense-prediction outputs show late-arriving fine detail; but the timing is described per setup, with no invariant that transfers across schedules and architectures.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The controlling clock for spectral acquisition is accumulated effective step size (the integral of LR over steps), not raw steps or epochs; after this reparameterization, frequency-band error trajectories from different schedules and reasonable architecture variants collapse onto one curve, because band ordering is set by loss-surface curvature per band, which the LR integral traverses at schedule-independent order.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across cosine/step/constant schedules and two architectures on NYU Depth v2, band-resolved error curves plotted against integrated LR will collapse with inter-configuration spread under 25% of the spread observed in raw-step time; the collapse will hold for at least 4 of 5 frequency bands. Kill the idea if integrated-LR reparameterization reduces spread by less than a factor of 1.5 or if architectures require separate curves (no universality).
why_important: A universal clock for detail acquisition lets practitioners predict when fine structure will arrive under any schedule, decide budget truncation rationally, and gives theorists a clean empirical invariant connecting curvature spectra to training dynamics in real dense models.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spectral-bias timing is studied in toy regression; the integrated-LR collapse test on real dense tasks appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train U-Net and DPT-style models on NYU Depth v2 under three schedules; compute wavelet-band residual errors at dense checkpoints; test trajectory collapse under raw-time vs integrated-LR parameterization.
main_risk: Adam's adaptive scaling blurs what counts as effective step size; running SGD variants (where integrated LR is well-defined) first, then testing Adam analogues (integrated global scale), keeps the claim testable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Detail acquisition timing is treated as architecture- and schedule-specific, requiring empirical tuning per setup.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Band curvature spectra may themselves evolve differently under different schedules (curvature is trajectory-dependent), breaking any single-clock account.
fastest_falsification_experiment: U-Net R50 and DPT (public) on NYU Depth v2 (public), 3 schedules x 2 architectures x 1 seed with dense checkpoints: about 3 days on one RTX 4090; band analysis is post-hoc.

one_line_idea: Within-class appearance variance, not class frequency, is the dominant determinant of when a class is acquired during segmentation training, inverting the standard imbalance-centric account of late learners.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Some classes are learned much later than others in dense training, and lateness is conventionally attributed to class rarity, motivating frequency-based reweighting and sampling remedies.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Acquisition time is governed by how many distinct appearance modes a class spans (its within-class feature variance): a rare but visually homogeneous class is learned quickly, while a frequent but heterogeneous class lags; frequency matters only through exposure count per appearance mode, so variance-per-exposure is the real clock.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across Cityscapes and ADE20K, partial correlation of class acquisition epoch (first epoch reaching 80% of final class IoU) with measured within-class feature variance, controlling for frequency, will exceed 0.5, while the reverse partial (frequency controlling variance) will be under 0.25; engineered homogeneous-rare vs heterogeneous-frequent class subsets will confirm the ordering. Kill the idea if the frequency partial dominates (>= 0.45 and larger than the variance partial) on both datasets.
why_important: If variance drives acquisition, remedies for late classes should target mode coverage (sampling per appearance mode) rather than raw frequency amplification, redirecting a whole family of imbalance interventions toward the actually operative variable.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Class-difficulty analyses report correlations with frequency and size; a controlled partial-correlation adjudication with engineered class subsets appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compute per-class acquisition epochs from dense checkpoints; measure within-class variance using a frozen pretrained embedder; run partial correlations both ways; build two engineered subset datasets that decouple the variables and re-train.
main_risk: Feature-variance measurement depends on the embedder; using two unrelated public embedders and requiring agreement protects the statistic.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Late acquisition is explained by rarity, as encoded in ubiquitous frequency-reweighting defaults.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Variance and frequency are correlated in real datasets, and the engineered decoupling may create unnatural co-occurrence statistics that change acquisition for other reasons.

one_line_idea: Delayed generalization (grokking-like) exists in dense prediction: under strong weight decay and small data, validation boundary quality jumps long after training loss saturates, with the delay controlled by the decay strength.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Delayed generalization long after training-set fit (grokking) is documented for algorithmic and some classification tasks; whether dense prediction exhibits the phenomenon, and in which output structures, is unknown.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense tasks have instance-idiosyncratic fit components (exact boundary placements on small training sets) and generalizable components (region semantics); with small data and strong decay, networks first fit boundaries idiosyncratically, then slowly consolidate to transferable boundary rules under the decay pressure, producing a late jump in validation boundary metrics while interior metrics track training loss conventionally.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On 500-image Pascal VOC subsets with weight decay at 10x standard, validation boundary F-score will improve by at least 5 points after the epoch where training loss has been within 1% of its final value for 100+ epochs, and the delay length will scale monotonically with decay strength across 3 levels; interior accuracy will show no comparable late jump (< 1 point). Kill the idea if no late boundary improvement above 2 points occurs at any decay level, or the delay does not vary with decay.
why_important: Extending delayed-generalization phenomenology to dense outputs would show that structured outputs have separable idiosyncratic-fit and consolidation phases by output region, informing early-stopping policy (stopping at train saturation discards the late consolidation) and connecting dense training to a growing dynamical literature.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Grokking studies concentrate on algorithmic/classification data; a region-resolved dense version with decay-controlled delay appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Small-data segmentation runs at 3 decay levels x 3 seeds with very long budgets and dense evaluation; decompose validation improvements into boundary bands vs interiors; measure delay statistics.
main_risk: Very long small-data runs are cheap per step but numerous; the phenomenon may also require specific data sizes, needing a small size ladder to find the operative regime.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense training is assumed to generalize (or not) monotonically with training progress, with nothing left to gain long after training loss saturates.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The boundary-consolidation story may be wishful: late validation movement could be evaluation noise, which the 5-point bar and seed replication are set to filter.
fastest_falsification_experiment: U-Net R18 (public encoder) on 500-image VOC subsets (public), 9 runs x 2000 epochs at low resolution: about 3 days on one RTX 4090.

one_line_idea: Early training at low resolution creates a persistent thin-structure deficit that equal-compute high-resolution fine-tuning cannot repair, establishing a within-run critical period for spatial detail.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Progressive-resolution training (start small, finish large) is a common efficiency recipe, assumed lossless because final epochs see full resolution.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Filters and attention patterns that resolve thin structures must form while gradients from those structures exist; at low resolution thin structures vanish from supervision, and the network commits capacity to coarse solutions that later high-resolution gradients only locally patch rather than restructure, leaving a permanent deficit relative to full-resolution-throughout training at matched total compute.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Progressive training (50% resolution for the first half) will end at least 2 IoU below full-resolution training on Cityscapes thin classes (pole, traffic sign/light) at matched compute, with the deficit shrinking by less than half when the high-resolution phase is doubled, while blob-class IoU matches within 0.3. Kill the idea if the thin-class deficit is under 0.8 IoU, or if doubling the high-res phase eliminates it (no critical period, just insufficient budget).
why_important: Progressive resolution is widely used to cut cost; a real critical period would mean the savings silently tax exactly the classes many applications care most about, and would be among the cleanest demonstrations that acquisition order constrains what is ultimately learnable within standard budgets.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Critical-period phenomena are shown for early-training deficits in classification; a resolution-specific, class-resolved version for dense prediction appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compare full-resolution, progressive, and extended-progressive schedules at matched compute on Cityscapes; report class-resolved IoU with thin-class stratification; probe first-layer/early-block frequency selectivity at the switch point and end.
main_risk: Matched-compute accounting between resolutions has freedom (per-image vs per-pixel compute); pre-registering FLOP-matched budgets removes the ambiguity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The final training resolution is assumed to determine final detail capability, making progressive schedules a free lunch.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern architectures with strong multi-scale features may retain enough plasticity for the late phase to fully restructure, erasing the deficit and revealing the critical period as an artifact of older architectures.

one_line_idea: Attention-map organization in ViT-based dense models undergoes an abrupt within-run transition (entropy drop plus locality emergence), and dense-task transferability of the features begins rising only after this transition, making it a measurable readiness marker.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Trained ViTs show structured attention (locality in early layers, object-aligned patterns later); when this structure forms during dense training and what it gates is not established.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Attention organization is a phase transition rather than gradual drift: token-attention entropy drops sharply within a narrow step window as heads differentiate, and until this reorganization happens the features are poorly transferable to dense readouts; the transition time therefore separates an unproductive warm phase from a productive representation phase, and interventions that accelerate the transition (locality-biased init) shift the whole accuracy curve forward.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training SegFormer-style/ViT dense models from scratch on ADE20K subsets, mean attention entropy will complete at least 60% of its total drop within a window of at most 10% of training steps, frozen-feature dense-probe accuracy will begin its main rise within 5% of steps after that window in at least 3 of 4 runs, and locality-biased initialization will shift both events earlier by at least 20%. Kill the idea if the entropy drop is spread over more than 40% of training (no transition) or probe-rise timing is uncoupled from it.
why_important: A measurable readiness marker for dense representations enables schedule decisions (when fine-tuning phases can start, when to enable auxiliary objectives) keyed to internal state rather than step counts, and characterizes a genuine nonlinearity in dense-training dynamics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Attention-structure analyses exist on finished models and language-model phase transitions are reported; the coupling of an attention transition to dense transferability timing appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: From-scratch ViT dense training with dense checkpointing; track attention entropy per layer and frozen-feature probe accuracy; test event coupling and the init intervention.
main_risk: From-scratch ViT training on segmentation-scale data is unstable; using ImageNet-100 pretraining as the observed run (with dense probes) is a fallback that preserves the coupling question.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Representation quality is assumed to grow smoothly with training, without gating events worth scheduling around.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The entropy drop may be an epiphenomenon of LR warmup ending rather than an intrinsic reorganization, which the init intervention (which does not change warmup) is designed to expose.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ViT-S trained on ImageNet-100 (public) with ADE20K (public) dense probes at checkpoints, plus a locality-init arm, 2 seeds: about 3.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Class acquisition order in dense training is optimization-forced, not data-forced: aggressive class-balanced resampling shifts acquisition times but preserves the order, exposing a fixed difficulty hierarchy that data curricula cannot reorder.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Classes are acquired in a characteristic order during segmentation training, and data-centric practice implicitly assumes exposure schedules control what is learned when.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Acquisition order reflects intrinsic optimization difficulty (feature depth required, gradient signal geometry) rather than exposure statistics; resampling changes each class's clock speed but not the sequence, so even extreme rebalancing will fail to move early learners behind late learners, bounding what any within-run data curriculum can achieve.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under 10x class-balanced resampling on Cityscapes and ADE20K, the rank order of class acquisition epochs will correlate with the natural-sampling order at Kendall tau >= 0.7, with no class moving more than 2 rank positions in 3 of 4 runs, while absolute acquisition times shift by up to 40%. Kill the idea if tau < 0.45 or 3+ classes swap across the median rank, which would establish genuine data-forced ordering and validate curriculum control.
why_important: Either outcome is decision-relevant: order rigidity redirects effort from exposure curricula to loss/architecture interventions for late classes, while order plasticity would justify serious curriculum engineering; currently the community assumes plasticity without measurement.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resampling is evaluated by final accuracy, not by whether it reorders acquisition; the order-invariance test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train natural vs 10x-balanced sampling with dense checkpoints on both datasets; compute acquisition epochs per class; compare rank orders and time shifts across seeds.
main_risk: Acquisition-epoch estimates are noisy for classes with flat late curves; defining acquisition at multiple thresholds (60/80/90% of final IoU) makes the rank comparison robust.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] What the model learns first is assumed to follow what it sees most, motivating exposure-based curricula.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Extreme resampling may alter effective co-occurrence contexts enough to genuinely change difficulty (context is part of the signal), producing order changes for reasons beyond exposure counting.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes + ADE20K (public), 2 sampling arms x 2 datasets x 2 seeds with checkpointing: about 3 days on one A100.
