one_line_idea: Epoch-wise double descent in dense prediction is spatially localized: boundary-band validation error is non-monotone over training while interior error descends monotonically, so the phenomenon's visibility depends on which metric a paper reports.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Epoch-wise double descent (validation error rising then falling again with training time) is documented for classification under label corruption and capacity stress; its existence and structure in dense prediction is unmapped.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The idiosyncratic-fit-then-consolidation dynamics that produce epoch-wise double descent operate on the hardest, most idiosyncratic pixels, which concentrate near boundaries; interiors are learned smoothly. Dense double descent therefore exists but hides inside spatially aggregated metrics, explaining why it is rarely reported for segmentation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Training compact models on reduced Cityscapes (capacity-stressed regime), 8px-boundary-band validation error will show a rise of at least 3% relative followed by recovery in at least 3 of 4 seeds, while interior error rises by under 1% at the same epochs; aggregate mIoU will show a rise of under 1% (masked phenomenon). Kill the idea if no band shows non-monotonicity above noise (2x seed standard deviation) in any capacity-stressed configuration tested.
why_important: It locates a canonical deep-learning phenomenon inside structured outputs, warns that aggregate dense metrics can mask non-monotone generalization (checkpoint selection implications), and identifies boundary pixels as the idiosyncrasy-sensitive population in dense training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Double-descent studies target classification and simple regression; a spatially-resolved dense version appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Capacity-stressed segmentation runs (small models, reduced data, long budgets) with dense evaluation; decompose validation error into boundary bands vs interiors over time; replicate across 4 seeds and 2 capacity levels.
main_risk: The phenomenon may require label corruption to appear at practical scales; a corrupted-boundary arm is a fallback that changes the claim's scope but keeps the spatial-localization question intact.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Dense-task validation curves are assumed monotone under standard settings, so no one schedules or selects checkpoints around a mid-training degradation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Boundary error may be dominated by irreducible placement noise that drowns a small non-monotone component below the pre-registered detection bar.
fastest_falsification_experiment: U-Net R18 (public) on quarter-size Cityscapes (public), 2 capacities x 4 seeds x long budgets at low resolution: about 3 days on one RTX 4090; band decomposition is post-hoc.

one_line_idea: Within-run neural collapse in segmentation heads is class-asymmetric: frequent-class features collapse toward their class means early while rare-class features never fully collapse, and the residual within-class variance identifies which classes still benefit from continued training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Neural collapse (within-class feature variance shrinking to class means at the end of classification training) is documented for balanced classification; its dynamics in imbalanced dense prediction heads are uncharted.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Collapse progress per class is set by effective gradient exposure, so dense heads exhibit a moving frontier: frequent classes reach near-collapse early (after which their accuracy is optimizer-noise-bound), rare classes remain far from collapse at budget end (data/exposure-bound); the per-class collapse gap therefore partitions classes into those that longer training can still help and those needing other interventions.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes, the within-class-to-between-class variance ratio in the penultimate head features will differ by at least 4x between the most and least frequent class quintiles at budget end, per-class IoU gains from 2x budget extension will concentrate (>= 70%) in classes above the median residual-variance, and frequent-quintile gains will be under 0.3 IoU. Kill the idea if the collapse ratio spread is under 1.5x, or budget-extension gains are uncorrelated with residual variance (rho < 0.25).
why_important: It imports a precise theoretical object (collapse geometry) into dense training as a practical training-sufficiency diagnostic per class, replacing guesswork about whether longer training will help with a measurable geometric criterion.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Neural collapse under imbalance is studied theoretically for classification (minority collapse); a within-run, per-class diagnostic application to dense heads appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument segmentation training to record per-class feature statistics in the head; compute collapse trajectories; extend budget 2x and attribute per-class gains against residual variance at the original endpoint.
main_risk: Pixel features are spatially correlated, so variance statistics need subsampled, decorrelated pixel sets to avoid trivially inflated within-class variance for large-region classes.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Longer training is assumed to lift all boats slowly, without a geometric criterion for which classes remain trainable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Rare-class residual variance may reflect genuine multi-modality that no amount of training collapses, decoupling the diagnostic from budget-extension gains.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), instrumented run + 2x-budget extension x 2 seeds: about 2.5 days on one A100; feature statistics are computed online at negligible cost.

one_line_idea: Interior and boundary pixels of the same instance send systematically conflicting gradients through shared decoder features, and the depth at which the conflict peaks tells you where decoupled decoding pays off.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Segmentation decoders process all pixels through shared features, and architectures with separate boundary streams sometimes help; when and where separation is warranted is decided by trial and error.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Boundary pixels need high-frequency, position-sensitive features while interiors need smoothed semantic evidence; through shared channels these demands produce negatively-aligned gradient components whose magnitude is layer-localized (largest in mid-decoder), so splitting only the layers above the measured conflict peak captures the benefit of dual-stream designs at a fraction of the parameters.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Per-layer cosine between interior-pixel and boundary-pixel gradient aggregates will be below -0.1 in a contiguous mid-decoder band and near zero elsewhere across two architectures, and splitting decoders only above the conflict peak will recover at least 70% of the full dual-stream mIoU gain with under 30% of its parameter overhead. Kill the idea if conflict cosines are everywhere above -0.03 (no structured conflict) or split-at-peak recovers under 30% of the dual-stream gain.
why_important: It grounds boundary-stream architecture folklore in a measurable optimization quantity, turns an architecture search into a one-run diagnostic, and adds evidence that spatial populations within one task behave like conflicting tasks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-conflict analysis is standard across tasks in multi-task learning; applying population-conflict profiling within a single dense task to place architectural splits appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument DeepLabv3+ and SegFormer training with per-layer population-gradient cosines (interior vs 8px boundary band); train full dual-stream and split-at-peak variants; compare gains and costs.
main_risk: Population gradients aggregated per layer may hide channel-level structure; a channel-resolved follow-up is the natural refinement if layer-level conflict is weak.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Boundary streams are motivated representationally (edges need their own features), with no optimization-conflict measurement behind the design choice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Conflict may be beneficial regularization rather than harm, in which case splitting at the conflict peak could reduce accuracy despite faithful conflict measurements.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), instrumented baselines + 2 split variants x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Deep-supervision auxiliary heads work as per-depth gradient-norm equalizers, so removing them and directly rescaling per-block learning rates to match their induced gradient profile should reproduce their accuracy, collapsing an architectural ritual into an optimizer setting.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Auxiliary segmentation heads at intermediate layers (deep supervision) are standard in classic pipelines and persist in modern ones, explained loosely as helping gradient flow or intermediate representation quality.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The operative effect of auxiliary heads is to raise effective gradient magnitude at earlier blocks, compensating depth attenuation; the representational content of the auxiliary task is largely irrelevant, so per-block LR rescaling matched to the measured with-aux gradient-norm profile will reproduce the benefit without any auxiliary computation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Profile-matched per-block LR rescaling will recover at least 70% of the auxiliary head's mIoU gain on both PSPNet-style and modern configs, and an auxiliary head with a content-degraded target (heavily blurred labels) will retain at least 60% of the standard auxiliary gain, jointly implicating magnitude over content. Kill the idea if LR matching recovers under 30% of the gain or the degraded-target head loses most of it (content matters after all).
why_important: Auxiliary heads cost memory and complicate architecture; proving them equivalent to an optimizer profile removes a ritual, while a kill (content matters) upgrades deep supervision from folklore to a representational claim worth designing deliberately.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Deep supervision is ubiquitous but its mechanism is asserted, not decomposed; the profile-matching and content-degradation controls appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure per-block gradient norms with and without auxiliary heads; train arms {no-aux, aux, LR-profile-matched no-aux, degraded-target aux} at matched budgets; compare mIoU over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Auxiliary heads also change BN statistics along the side branch; using GN variants or excluding branch statistics isolates the gradient pathway.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Deep supervision is believed to inject useful intermediate semantic pressure, a content-based account.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Intermediate supervision may genuinely shape feature content (forcing early semantic separability) in ways an LR profile cannot, which the degraded-target arm will reveal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: PSPNet-R50 (public, mmsegmentation) on ADE20K (public), 4 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Optimal task weights in multi-task dense training are those that equalize per-task gradient noise-to-signal ratios measured mid-run, replacing grid search over weights with a two-measurement rule.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Multi-task dense training requires task-weight tuning that consumes most of the practical effort; automatic weighting schemes exist but disagree with each other and with grid-search optima across setups.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Late training is noise-floor-limited: the task whose gradient noise dominates the shared parameters sets everyone's plateau, so the weight vector that equalizes per-task noise-to-signal ratios (gradient variance over squared mean, measured on shared parameters mid-run) coincides with the grid-search optimum; existing schemes work exactly when they approximate this equalization.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On seg+depth and seg+normals NYU Depth v2 setups, the noise-equalizing weights computed from one mid-run measurement will land within the grid-search optimal region (within 0.5% combined metric of the grid optimum) in at least 3 of 4 cases, and grid optima will show equalized measured ratios (within 2x) while clearly suboptimal weights show ratios apart by 5x+. Kill the idea if the equalizing weights miss the optimal region by more than 2% combined metric in half the cases, or optima do not exhibit ratio equalization.
why_important: It offers a mechanistic account of what task-weight tuning actually finds, compresses an expensive search into two measurements, and adjudicates between competing automatic-weighting stories with a single falsifiable criterion.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Homoscedastic-weighting-style and gradient-norm-based schemes exist; the specific noise-to-signal equalization law tested against grid-search ground truth appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid-search task weights on two dense pairs to locate optima; measure per-task gradient statistics on shared parameters at several weights; test whether equalization predicts the optimum location.
main_risk: Gradient statistics drift over training, so the measurement time matters; testing at three measurement points establishes whether a single mid-run snapshot suffices.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Task weighting is treated as an empirical search problem or delegated to heuristic schemes with no agreed governing quantity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Early-phase trajectory effects (which task leads learning) may set final outcomes in ways invisible to late-phase noise ratios, breaking the single-snapshot rule.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ResNet-50 multi-task models (public implementations) on NYU Depth v2 (public), 7-point weight grids x 2 pairs x 2 seeds at 10 epochs: about 3 days on one RTX 4090; statistics measurement adds negligible cost.

one_line_idea: Cross-view consistency gradients in augmentation-consistency training act as beneficial exploration noise early and harmful drag late, predicting that the standard constant or ramp-up consistency weight is backwards at the end of training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Consistency objectives between augmented views are core to semi- and self-supervised dense training, scheduled with constant weights or ramp-ups fixed by folklore.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Disagreement between views carries two components: informative invariance signal and augmentation-artifact noise; early, both push features usefully (exploration plus invariance), but late in training the artifact component dominates residual disagreement (real invariances are already learned), so consistency gradients increasingly conflict with the supervised signal at low LR, and decaying the consistency weight in the last phase should beat both constant and ramp schedules.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On semi-supervised Cityscapes (1/8 labels) with a standard teacher-student consistency setup, late-phase decay of the consistency weight will beat the tuned-constant baseline by at least 0.7 mIoU, the measured cosine between consistency and supervised gradients will decline over training by at least 0.15, and reversing the schedule (ramping consistency up at the end) will lose at least 1.0 mIoU. Kill the idea if the gradient cosine does not decline or late decay fails to beat tuned-constant by more than 0.2 mIoU.
why_important: Consistency weights are among the most-tuned constants in label-efficient dense learning; a phase-dependent law with a measurable driver (gradient alignment decay) converts that tuning into a principled schedule and clarifies what consistency training is doing when it stops helping.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ramp-up folklore is documented in classic semi-supervised methods; the late-phase alignment-decay measurement and decay-schedule prescription for dense tasks appear new. Distinct from occupied W13-P1-F-036 (teacher quality moderating pseudo-label format), this idea concerns the within-run temporal role of the consistency term itself.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train semi-supervised segmentation with {constant, ramp-up, late-decay, late-ramp} consistency schedules at matched exposure; log consistency-supervised gradient cosines; compare mIoU over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Teacher EMA dynamics entangle with the consistency weight; pinning the EMA constant across arms keeps the manipulated variable clean.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Consistency pressure is assumed neutral-to-helpful throughout training, hence constant or increasing schedules everywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Late consistency disagreement may concentrate exactly on the hard boundary pixels where supervision is scarce, making it late-phase signal rather than noise and reversing the prescription.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 mean-teacher setup (public implementations) on Cityscapes 1/8-label split (public protocol), 4 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: The classification and box-regression branches of dense detectors conflict on shared features with a characteristic time signature (regression gradients shrink as boxes converge while classification persists), explaining mechanistically why decoupled-head designs win and when they stop mattering.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Decoupling detection heads (separate towers for classification and regression) reliably improves one-stage detectors, an empirical finding adopted without a dynamical explanation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Early in training both branches need coarse localization features and their gradients align; as boxes converge, regression gradients shrink and rotate toward high-frequency refinement directions while classification gradients keep demanding invariant semantic features, so branch conflict on shared features grows over training; the benefit of decoupling therefore accrues late, scales with the measured late-phase conflict, and disappears for short schedules.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Branch-gradient cosine on shared tower features will decline from positive to below -0.05 over training in coupled heads across RetinaNet and FCOS, decoupling's AP gain will be at least 3x larger at full schedule than at a 25% schedule, and per-phase swap experiments (couple early, decouple late) will capture at least 80% of the full decoupling gain. Kill the idea if the cosine stays positive throughout, or if decoupling's gain is budget-independent (within 20%), or late-only decoupling captures under 40%.
why_important: It converts a widely copied architecture trick into a dynamical law with schedule-dependent predictions, and the late-only-decoupling recipe (shared early, split late) would reduce head cost during most of training if the phase account is right.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Decoupled heads are established practice; the temporal conflict signature and phase-swap decomposition appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument coupled-head training with branch-gradient cosines; train coupled, decoupled, and phase-swap variants at two budgets on COCO; compare AP patterns against the conflict trajectories.
main_risk: Centerness/objectness branches complicate the two-branch story in some detectors; choosing RetinaNet (clean two-branch) as the primary subject keeps the test sharp.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Decoupled heads are believed to work because the two subtasks simply need different features, a static account with no schedule prediction.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The benefit may come from doubled head capacity rather than conflict removal; a widened-coupled-head control at matched parameters directly tests this rival.

one_line_idea: In panoptic training, stuff-region gradients numerically dominate thing-region gradients through sheer pixel count, suppressing instance-discrimination learning; branch-specific batch composition (alternating thing-rich and stuff-rich crops) should fix this without any loss reweighting.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Panoptic and instance-aware models train thing (countable object) and stuff (region) recognition through shared features, and thing-related metrics typically lag; remedies focus on loss weights and head designs.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The lag is partly a gradient-budget artifact: stuff regions contribute most supervised pixels per batch, so shared features drift toward stuff-optimal statistics between sparse thing-gradient events; composing batches to alternate thing-dense and stuff-dense crops concentrates thing gradients into coherent updates (less inter-batch dilution), improving thing performance at equal data and loss settings.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Alternating-composition batching will improve thing-class panoptic quality (PQ-things) by at least 1.5 points on COCO-panoptic at unchanged loss weights, with stuff PQ within 0.5 points of baseline, and the measured thing-gradient share per batch will roughly double under the composition change. Kill the idea if PQ-things improves by under 0.5, or if matching the same thing-gradient share via loss reweighting achieves the same gain (composition adds nothing beyond reweighting).
why_important: It locates part of a well-known performance asymmetry in batch-composition dynamics rather than loss design, and offers a data-scheduling fix orthogonal to the heavily explored weighting/architecture axes, with a built-in control that adjudicates composition against reweighting.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Thing/stuff asymmetry is discussed via losses and architectures; the batch-composition timing mechanism with a reweighting-equivalence control appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Panoptic FPN training with standard vs alternating-composition batching vs gradient-share-matched reweighting on COCO-panoptic; log per-batch thing/stuff gradient shares; compare PQ decompositions over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Crop composition changes object-scale statistics simultaneously; matching crop-scale distributions across arms isolates the composition timing variable.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Thing-stuff imbalance is treated as a loss-weighting problem, with batch composition considered interchangeable as long as the epoch-level distribution matches.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If momentum and Adam smooth gradient timing sufficiently, epoch-level composition is all that matters and the alternating scheme will match plain shuffling.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Panoptic FPN R50 (public, detectron2) on COCO-panoptic (public) at 1x schedule, 3 arms x 2 seeds: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Teacher-student dense self-distillation has a two-phase structure with a measurable phase boundary: before teacher-student agreement crosses a threshold the teacher acts as a denoiser, after it the loop locks in student errors, so distillation weight should be scheduled against measured agreement, not time.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Mean-teacher-style self-distillation for dense tasks feeds a moving average of the student back as a target; confirmation of student errors is a known qualitative risk, managed by hand-tuned schedules.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] While teacher-student disagreement is high, teacher targets carry independent-enough information to denoise the student; once agreement exceeds a threshold, the residual teacher signal is dominated by the student's own systematic errors reflected back, and continued distillation pressure entrenches them; the transition is detectable online as the point where teacher-corrections stop correlating with ground-truth error reduction on a small labeled probe.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] In semi-supervised Cityscapes distillation, the correlation between accepted teacher-corrections and probe-measured error reduction will decay from significantly positive to near zero as pixel-level agreement passes a threshold (within a 5-point agreement window consistent across seeds), and cutting distillation weight at the measured crossing will beat the best fixed schedule by at least 0.5 mIoU. Kill the idea if the correlation shows no agreement-linked decay, or measured-crossing cutoff fails to beat fixed schedules by more than 0.1 mIoU.
why_important: It replaces open-loop distillation schedules with a closed-loop rule based on an observable, and quantifies the onset of self-confirmation, the central failure mode of self-training, as a reproducible transition rather than an anecdote.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Confirmation bias in self-training is discussed qualitatively; an online agreement-threshold law with a closed-loop cutoff test appears untested. Distinct from occupied W13-P1-F-036 (soft/hard pseudo-label format moderated by teacher quality): here the subject is the temporal feedback-loop dynamics of the within-run loop, not label format.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrumented mean-teacher training with a held-out labeled probe; track agreement, correction-utility correlation, and run cutoff-at-crossing vs fixed-schedule arms over 2 seeds.
main_risk: The labeled probe must be small to keep the semi-supervised setting honest; correlation estimates on small probes are noisy, requiring temporal smoothing that could blur the transition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Distillation strength schedules are set by time-based heuristics, with confirmation risk managed by confidence thresholds rather than loop-state measurements.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Agreement may saturate so early that the useful-denoising phase is negligible in modern setups, making the schedule question moot (also an informative outcome).
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 mean-teacher (public implementations) on Cityscapes 1/8-label protocol (public), instrumented run + 3 schedule arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Cut-and-paste mixing augmentations shift a large share of the boundary-gradient budget onto artificial paste boundaries, so their net effect flips sign between interior-dominated and boundary-sensitive evaluation, resolving contradictory reports about their value for segmentation.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] CutMix-style and copy-paste augmentations improve segmentation and detection in many reports, with occasional contrary findings, and the boundary pixels they synthesize do not correspond to true object boundaries.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Pasted edges are high-loss, high-gradient regions that compete directly with true-boundary learning for the boundary-gradient budget; the augmentation therefore helps interior/context robustness while systematically taxing true-boundary precision, and the net effect on any benchmark is predicted by the benchmark metric's boundary sensitivity.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under CutMix-style training on Cityscapes, artificial boundaries will absorb at least 25% of total boundary-band gradient, interior-region accuracy will improve by at least 0.5 points while 4px-trimap boundary F-score drops by at least 1.0 point, and a variant that masks the loss in a thin band around paste edges will retain the interior gains while halving the boundary tax. Kill the idea if boundary metrics do not degrade (drop < 0.3) under standard mixing, or the paste-band gradient share is under 10% (no meaningful budget capture).
why_important: It explains sign flips in the mixing-augmentation literature via one measurable channel, and the band-masking fix is immediately deployable, converting a controversial augmentation into a controllable tradeoff.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mixing augmentations are heavily studied at the metric level; the boundary-gradient-budget accounting and band-masked variant appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train with/without CutMix and with band-masked CutMix on Cityscapes and VOC; log gradient shares by band type (true boundary, paste boundary, interior); decompose accuracy by region.
main_risk: Paste-edge effects depend on mask blending style (hard vs feathered); testing both bounds the claim's scope.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mixing augmentations are regarded as generically beneficial regularizers for dense tasks, with boundary effects unexamined.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Networks may learn to identify paste artifacts quickly, spending negligible late-phase gradient there, in which case the tax vanishes after warm phases and the sign-flip account fails.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes + Pascal VOC (public), 3 arms x 2 datasets x 2 seeds at 40k/20k iterations: about 3 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Frozen-BN folklore in detection fine-tuning works because small-batch BN statistic noise acts as an uncontrolled multiplicative perturbation on all downstream computation, so noise-corrected BN (larger virtual batches) should erase the freezing advantage and flip the recommendation at scale.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Detection fine-tuning recipes freeze backbone BN layers by default, a decade-old folklore justified by small per-GPU batch sizes, and carried unchanged into regimes where it may no longer apply.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The harm from live BN at small batches is statistic noise (batch mean/variance estimates jitter), which multiplies activations and destabilizes fine-tuning atop converged features; the harm is therefore a monotone function of statistic noise, so live BN with synchronized or accumulated statistics (large virtual batch) should match or beat frozen BN, and frozen BN should actively hurt when data statistics differ from pretraining.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On COCO Faster R-CNN fine-tuning at per-GPU batch 2, frozen BN will beat live BN by at least 1.0 AP, but live BN with virtual batch 32 (accumulated statistics) will come within 0.3 AP of frozen and beat it by at least 0.5 AP on a target set with shifted low-level statistics (different capture conditions subset). Kill the idea if noise-corrected live BN still trails frozen BN by more than 0.7 AP (freezing does more than remove statistic noise), or frozen BN wins even under strong statistic mismatch.
why_important: The freeze ritual is applied universally, including where it is likely counterproductive; a noise-based account gives the boundary (statistic noise vs statistics mismatch) and modern hardware makes the corrected alternative practical.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] The freeze default is well known; the decomposition into statistic-noise vs statistic-mismatch channels with a virtual-batch adjudication appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {frozen, live, live+virtual-batch} x {matched-statistics target, shifted-statistics target subset} on COCO fine-tuning; log BN statistic variance per arm; compare AP.
main_risk: Virtual-batch BN implementations differ (sync vs accumulation vs precise-BN recomputation); testing two implementations guards the conclusion against implementation artifacts.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Freezing BN is considered strictly safer for fine-tuning, an unconditional recipe rule.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Freezing may additionally act as beneficial regularization (fixing feature scales), a channel the noise correction cannot reproduce, which would keep frozen BN ahead and kill the idea informatively.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Faster R-CNN R50 (public, mmdetection) on COCO (public) with a shifted-statistics evaluation subset built from COCO metadata, 6 arms x 2 seeds at 1x schedule: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: BN running-statistics momentum is an implicit schedule that should be tied to the LR schedule: as LR decays, statistics lag the (now slowly moving) weights less, so the fixed default momentum over-smooths late training and under-smooths early training, and matching the two schedules removes a persistent train-eval gap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] BN maintains running statistics with a fixed momentum (typically 0.1) for evaluation, while training uses batch statistics; late-training evaluation metrics for dense models often jitter or lag training behavior, usually attributed to generic noise.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The optimal statistics-averaging window depends on how fast the underlying activations drift, which is set by the LR schedule; a fixed momentum is therefore wrong twice (too long a memory early when activations move fast, too short late when they are nearly static and noise dominates), and scheduling BN momentum proportionally to LR aligns the estimator with the drift rate, shrinking the train-eval gap and its jitter.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] LR-proportional BN momentum will reduce late-training evaluation jitter (standard deviation of val mIoU across the last 20 checkpoints) by at least 40% and improve final selected-checkpoint mIoU by at least 0.3 on Cityscapes small-batch training, with the measured statistics-lag (distance between running and instantaneous-precise statistics) reduced at least 2x late. Kill the idea if jitter reduction is under 15%, or precise-BN recomputation at each checkpoint (the gold standard) shows no gap for fixed momentum in the first place.
why_important: It identifies a silent coupling between two schedules everyone sets independently, offers a zero-cost recipe improvement, and explains a source of checkpoint-selection noise that plagues small-batch dense training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Precise-BN (recomputing statistics) is a known evaluation fix; scheduling the running momentum against LR as a within-run law appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {fixed momentum, LR-proportional momentum, precise-BN recompute} on small-batch Cityscapes training; measure statistics lag, val jitter, and final accuracy over 3 seeds.
main_risk: If precise-BN already solves everything cheaply, the scheduled-momentum contribution is redundant in practice, though the law about lag structure would still stand.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] BN momentum is a fixed constant of the layer, unrelated to the LR schedule.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Late-phase evaluation jitter may be dominated by genuine decision-boundary oscillation (weight-space), not statistics estimation, leaving momentum scheduling without a target.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public) at batch 4, 3 arms x 3 seeds at 40k iterations: about 2.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: The BN-vs-GN choice for dense training is governed by a two-dimensional phase boundary in (images per batch, pixels per image): BN wins only above a critical image count that itself grows with resolution, giving a chartable decision diagram instead of contradictory folklore.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] GroupNorm is known to beat BN at small batch sizes, and BN to win at large ones, but dense training varies both image count and per-image pixel count, and recipes carry normalization choices between regimes where the folklore was never validated.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] BN's statistic quality depends on effective sample diversity per batch, which for dense features is driven by image count (pixels within an image are correlated and add little), while GN's cost is discarding cross-image statistics; therefore the BN-GN crossover sits at an image-count threshold that is nearly independent of pixel count, predicting BN's regime shrinks at high resolution where memory forces low image counts, and the whole plane is chartable with a modest grid.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a (batch images {2,4,8,16}) x (resolution {512, 768, 1024}) grid on Cityscapes, the BN-GN accuracy crossover will occur at an image count consistent across resolutions within one grid step, while a pixels-per-batch account would predict crossover shifts of 2+ steps that will not materialize. Kill the idea if the crossover tracks total pixels rather than image count (shifting systematically with resolution), or if no stable crossover exists (interaction dominated by LR coupling).
why_important: It replaces a one-dimensional folklore with the actual decision surface practitioners face, and settles whether within-image pixels contribute meaningful normalization statistics, a question with consequences for all batch-statistic methods on dense features.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] BN-vs-GN batch-size curves exist for classification and detection at fixed resolution; the two-dimensional dense-task phase diagram with the image-count invariance claim appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the 12-cell grid with both normalizations at matched tuned LR per cell (small sweep), 1 seed per cell plus replicated boundary cells; locate crossovers per resolution row.
main_risk: Per-cell LR tuning is essential (BN and GN prefer different LRs) and dominates cost; skipping it would fabricate crossovers.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Normalization choice is guided by a single batch-size rule of thumb, assumed portable across resolutions and tasks.
why_it_might_be_wrong: High-resolution features may decorrelate enough spatially that within-image pixels do add statistic value, dragging the crossover along a pixels-per-batch contour instead.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 BN/GN variants (public) on Cityscapes (public), 12 cells x 2 norms x mini LR sweep at 20k iterations: about 5 days on one A100 40GB; the 2-resolution subgrid (2.5 days) already tests the invariance claim.

one_line_idea: fp16 training with loss scaling loses rare-class gradient contributions first, because their sparse, small-magnitude gradients sit closest to the underflow boundary, creating a class-selective precision tax that fp32 and bf16 do not share.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Mixed-precision (fp16 with dynamic loss scaling) is the default for dense training; its accuracy impact is audited at the aggregate-metric level, where it appears safely negligible.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Underflow in fp16 gradients is not class-neutral: rare classes contribute gradients that are both sparse and small (few pixels, often small structures), so a disproportionate fraction of their gradient mass falls below representable magnitude even with global loss scaling (which is set by the largest gradients); the resulting deficit is invisible in mIoU but measurable in rare-class IoU and in the fraction of underflowed gradient mass per class.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes with fp16+dynamic scaling vs bf16 vs fp32 at identical settings, rare-quintile class IoU will trail fp32 by at least 0.8 IoU under fp16 while frequent-quintile classes match within 0.2, per-class underflow accounting will show at least 5x higher underflowed-mass fraction for rare classes, and bf16 will match fp32 within 0.3 everywhere. Kill the idea if rare-class fp16 deficits are under 0.3 IoU or underflow mass shows no class asymmetry.
why_important: A class-selective precision tax would mean thousands of mixed-precision dense results carry a small systematic bias against exactly the classes applications care about, with a trivial fix (bf16 or per-class-aware scaling) once documented.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Mixed-precision audits check aggregate parity; class-resolved underflow accounting for dense training appears absent.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the three precision arms with per-class gradient underflow instrumentation (count masked gradient mass below fp16 min-normal per class at the head); compare class-quintile IoU across arms over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Dynamic loss scaling adapts over training, so underflow must be integrated across the run, and instrumentation must not itself alter scaling decisions.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mixed precision is regarded as accuracy-neutral for vision given loss scaling, full stop.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adam's normalization may rescue small gradients (the update direction survives even if magnitudes quantize), leaving no accuracy trace despite real underflow events.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 3 precision arms x 3 seeds at 40k iterations on an A100 (supports bf16): about 2.5 days; instrumentation is a backward-hook counter.

one_line_idea: Multi-resolution dense training works smoothly for LayerNorm architectures but silently degrades BN-based hybrids, because BN statistics are resolution-dependent while LN normalizes per token, predicting a normalization-conditioned verdict on variable-resolution schedules.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Variable-resolution and multi-scale training schedules are common for dense models, and are applied across architectures as if normalization were a neutral bystander.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Activation statistics at BN layers shift with input resolution (feature-map spatial statistics change with scale), so a batch mixing resolutions or a schedule alternating them forces BN running statistics to track a moving mixture, degrading both training stability and eval-time statistics fidelity; LN-family normalization is per-sample and scale-robust, so transformer-style models tolerate the same schedules, explaining anecdotal architecture-dependent reports about multi-scale training.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Under an alternating-resolution schedule on Cityscapes, a BN-based CNN will lose at least 1.0 mIoU relative to fixed-resolution training at matched compute while an LN-based transformer loses under 0.3, and per-resolution BN statistic distances will be at least 3x the within-resolution batch noise; per-resolution BN statistics (separate buffers per scale) will recover at least 70% of the BN loss. Kill the idea if BN and LN degrade equally (within 0.3), or per-resolution buffers recover under 30% (mechanism not statistics-based).
why_important: Multi-scale schedules are recommended generically; a normalization-conditioned rule prevents silent degradation in CNN pipelines and identifies the cheap fix (scale-specific statistics), while adding a concrete case to the growing map of normalization-schedule interactions.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Resolution-dependent BN statistics are folk-known in deployment (inference-resolution mismatch); the training-schedule version with the buffer-fix decomposition appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fixed vs alternating resolution schedules on {DeepLabv3+ (BN), SegFormer (LN)} with matched compute; log per-resolution statistic distances; add per-resolution-buffer BN arm; compare mIoU over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Compute matching between fixed and alternating schedules requires care (aspect ratios, crop content); FLOP-matched budgets with identical crop statistics per arm are pre-registered.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Multi-scale training is architecture-neutral good practice for dense robustness across scales.
why_it_might_be_wrong: BN's statistic mixing may act as beneficial scale-robustness regularization, actually helping generalization across evaluation resolutions and offsetting the fidelity loss.

one_line_idea: BN's train-mode stochasticity is a load-bearing regularizer in dense training: reproducing its measured noise distribution via explicit activation-noise injection under fixed statistics should recover most of BN's generalization advantage over deterministic normalization.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] BN outperforms deterministic alternatives in some dense regimes even when statistic-quality arguments favor the alternatives, hinting at a second mechanism beyond statistics estimation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Batch-statistic jitter perturbs every activation multiplicatively each step, a structured noise correlated within channels and batches; this noise regularizes like a channel-coherent dropout variant, and its contribution can be isolated by freezing statistics (removing estimation) while injecting noise matched to the measured jitter distribution, decomposing BN into estimator + regularizer.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes at batch 8, frozen-statistics BN with matched injected noise will recover at least 60% of the (live BN minus frozen-statistics BN) mIoU gap, and mismatched noise (white, channel-incoherent, same marginal variance) will recover under 25%, establishing that the correlation structure, not just the magnitude, carries the effect. Kill the idea if matched injection recovers under 25% of the gap (regularization channel negligible) or incoherent noise works just as well (structure irrelevant).
why_important: Decomposing BN's two roles lets architecture designers keep the regularization without batch coupling (injectable into GN/LN pipelines), and clarifies decade-old confusion about why BN sometimes wins beyond its statistic quality.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] BN-as-regularizer is a known qualitative claim; the measured-distribution injection test with a structure-matched vs unmatched control on dense tasks appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure BN statistic-jitter distributions during live training; run arms {live BN, frozen BN, frozen+matched-noise, frozen+white-noise}; compare mIoU and training curves over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Matching the full joint noise distribution is impossible; matching per-channel marginal plus batch-coherence structure is the pre-registered approximation, and its adequacy is itself informative.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] BN's benefit is attributed primarily to optimization smoothing and statistic estimation, with its noise treated as a side effect.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The regularization channel may only matter at small data scales; at Cityscapes scale both frozen arms may match live BN, nullifying the decomposition target.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 4 arms x 3 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3 days on one A100; jitter measurement is one instrumented epoch.

one_line_idea: In normalization-free dense training, adaptive gradient clipping thresholds map onto an equivalent BN batch-size curve, unifying two stability mechanisms as one effective constraint on relative update size and predicting threshold transfer across tasks without tuning.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Normalization-free networks stabilized by adaptive gradient clipping (bounding update-to-weight ratios) train competitively in classification, but porting them to dense tasks requires re-tuning the clipping threshold with no guidance on what it corresponds to.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Both BN and adaptive clipping ultimately bound the relative change a step can impose on a unit's computed function; if so, there is a mapping between clipping threshold and effective BN batch size that equalizes a measurable stability statistic (per-unit relative function change per step), and thresholds chosen by matching that statistic on a new dense task will be near-optimal without task-specific sweeps.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The relative-update statistic measured on stable BN baselines will identify a clipping threshold for the normalization-free variant within a factor of 2 of the sweep-optimal threshold on both Cityscapes segmentation and NYU Depth v2, with the statistic-matched run reaching within 0.5 mIoU/0.01 delta1 of the swept optimum. Kill the idea if the statistic-matched threshold misses the swept optimum by more than 4x or costs more than 1.5 mIoU, showing the two mechanisms are not exchangeable through this invariant.
why_important: A validated invariant would demystify stability tuning for normalization-free dense models (attractive for deployment reasons) and support a general principle: stability folklore across mechanisms reduces to bounding per-step relative function change.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Adaptive clipping for norm-free networks exists in classification; the cross-mechanism invariant and transfer rule for dense tasks appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure the relative-update statistic on BN baselines; sweep clipping thresholds for norm-free variants on two dense tasks; test whether statistic matching locates the optimum.
main_risk: Norm-free dense architectures are less standardized; adapting a public norm-free backbone to segmentation adds engineering that must be held fixed across arms.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Clipping thresholds are task-specific constants to be swept, unrelated to any normalization equivalent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Dense-task instabilities may be dominated by loss-surface events (rare high-loss crops) that clipping and BN handle differently, breaking any single-statistic equivalence.
fastest_falsification_experiment: NFNet-style backbone (public weights) with segmentation/depth heads on Cityscapes + NYU Depth v2 (public), threshold sweeps x 2 tasks at short schedules: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: bf16 and fp16 dense training differ mainly through loss-scaling dynamics rather than representational precision: fp16 with an oracle (perfect, non-adaptive) loss scale should match bf16, isolating the real cost of fp16 as scale-controller misbehavior during gradient-magnitude transients.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] bf16 is displacing fp16 for training stability, explained by exponent range; for dense vision the practical difference is confounded with the dynamic loss-scaling controller that fp16 requires and bf16 omits.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] fp16's mantissa is adequate for dense-vision gradients; its failures arise when the dynamic scaling controller reacts to gradient-magnitude transients (schedule changes, hard batches) with scale reductions that then underflow small gradients for thousands of steps; with a fixed oracle scale chosen post-hoc, fp16 matches bf16, implying the fix is controller design, not format switching, where bf16 hardware is unavailable.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes and COCO short-schedule training, fp16-with-oracle-scale will match bf16 within 0.2 mIoU/AP while standard dynamic-scaled fp16 shows at least one scale-reduction episode per run and trails by at least 0.4 in at least one setup; aligning scale-reduction episodes with underflow-mass spikes will show temporal coincidence (>= 80% of underflow mass within episode windows). Kill the idea if oracle-scaled fp16 still trails bf16 by more than 0.4 (mantissa/precision genuinely matters) or dynamic-scale runs show no episodes yet still trail.
why_important: It assigns blame precisely within mixed-precision folklore (controller vs format), guiding practitioners on fp16-only hardware toward better controllers instead of resignation, and documents how transient controller dynamics leave lasting accuracy marks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] bf16-vs-fp16 comparisons abound at the format level; the oracle-scale decomposition isolating controller dynamics on dense tasks appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {bf16, fp16-dynamic, fp16-oracle-fixed-scale} on two dense setups with underflow and scale-event logging; compare final metrics and episode-aligned underflow accounting over 2 seeds.
main_risk: The oracle scale must be discovered by pilot runs per setup; if no single fixed scale avoids both overflow and underflow across the run, the decomposition itself fails informatively (format range genuinely binds).
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] bf16's advantage is attributed to number format properties, with the scaling controller treated as a solved auxiliary detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention-heavy dense models may produce genuine fp16 overflow in activations (not gradients), a format limitation no gradient-scale oracle fixes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0 on Cityscapes and RetinaNet-R50 on COCO (public), 3 precision arms x 2 setups x 2 seeds at short schedules on an A100: about 3.5 days; logging is hook-based.

one_line_idea: Online hard-example mining is a feedback dynamical system with two regimes: a stable regime where the mined set evolves slowly and mining helps, and a limit-cycle regime where the mined set flips between populations and mining underperforms plain training, with the regime identifiable online from mined-set overlap.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] OHEM and hard-pixel mining sometimes improve dense training and sometimes destabilize it, with practitioners adjusting mining ratios by trial and error.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Mining couples model state to data selection: training on mined pixels lowers their loss, ejecting them from the mined set and re-admitting previously easy pixels whose loss rose from neglect; depending on mining ratio and LR this feedback settles (stable frontier) or oscillates (populations alternate); consecutive-epoch mined-set Jaccard overlap distinguishes the regimes, predicting mining's benefit sign without waiting for final metrics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across mining ratios {10%, 25%, 50%} and LRs on Cityscapes, runs with late-phase mined-set Jaccard >= 0.5 will beat their no-mining twins by at least 0.5 mIoU on average, runs with Jaccard <= 0.2 will trail by at least 0.3, and the overlap statistic measured at one-third of training will classify final benefit sign with at least 80% accuracy over 12 configurations. Kill the idea if benefit sign is uncorrelated with mined-set overlap (classification accuracy < 60%) or no configuration exhibits the low-overlap oscillation regime.
why_important: It reframes a widely used heuristic as a controllable dynamical system with an online health signal, letting practitioners auto-tune or abort mining instead of discovering failures at evaluation time, and connecting selection-feedback dynamics to measurable training outcomes.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] OHEM variants are abundant; treating mined-set persistence as a regime diagnostic with a pre-registered classification test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid mining ratio x LR with mined-set logging on Cityscapes; compute overlap trajectories; test the early-overlap classifier of final benefit against no-mining twins.
main_risk: Mined-set composition can drift with LR schedule independent of feedback; comparing against a frozen-model mining control (mine with a fixed snapshot) separates feedback dynamics from schedule drift.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Mining is viewed as a static emphasis choice whose failures are attributed to noisy labels or excessive ratios, not to an identifiable oscillation regime.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Momentum and Adam smoothing may damp the feedback everywhere in practical ranges, leaving only the stable regime and nothing to classify.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 12 mining configs + twins at 20k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100; overlap logging is nearly free.

one_line_idea: The crop-size folklore for segmentation decomposes into a normalization-statistics component and a context component, and controlled statistic-swapping shows which one carries the large-crop advantage, with opposite architectural implications.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training on larger crops improves segmentation accuracy in most reports, attributed by default to richer context; but crop size simultaneously changes BN statistic quality, pixel correlation per batch, and boundary-to-interior pixel ratios.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] A substantial share of the large-crop advantage flows through normalization statistics (larger crops give more stable per-batch activation statistics at fixed image count), not through longer-range context reaching the loss; swapping statistics across crop regimes (computing BN statistics from large crops while supervising small ones, and vice versa) will attribute the advantage between the two channels, and the context share will concentrate on large-object classes only.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes DeepLabv3+ (BN), statistic-swapped small-crop training will recover at least 40% of the large-crop advantage overall, the remaining context component will be at least 3x larger on the biggest-object classes than on small-object classes, and GroupNorm replication will shrink the statistics component below 15%. Kill the idea if statistic swapping moves accuracy by under 10% of the crop gap (statistics channel negligible) and the context component shows no class-size structure.
why_important: Crop size is among the most compute-expensive knobs in dense training; knowing that part of its benefit is a normalization artifact (cheaply replaceable) versus true context (worth paying for, but only for certain classes) changes how training pipelines spend memory.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crop-size effects are folklore-tier; the statistic-swap attribution design appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {small crop, large crop, small crop + large-crop statistics, large crop + small-crop statistics} under BN, plus GN replication; class-size-stratified accuracy decomposition over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Statistic swapping requires a two-stream implementation (supervision crops and statistics crops per batch), whose engineering must not alter effective batch composition.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Large crops help because context helps, an explanation applied uniformly across classes and normalization schemes.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The advantage may be dominated by a third channel, boundary-to-interior pixel ratio shifts in the loss, which the design should extend to monitor via band-resolved loss shares.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 BN/GN (public) on Cityscapes (public), 6 arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100 40GB.

one_line_idea: Per-pixel loss computation is massively redundant: the safe pixel-subsampling rate for loss evaluation is set by the spatial correlation length of the gradient field, giving a measurable dial that trades compute for nothing until a sharp knee.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense losses are computed at every labeled pixel by default; pixel-sampled losses appear in some methods for other reasons (noise robustness, class balance) but the pure-redundancy question, how few pixels suffice, lacks a governing quantity.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Neighboring pixels contribute nearly identical gradients through shared receptive fields, so the information content of the per-pixel loss field is governed by its spatial correlation length; random sampling at spacing below that length loses nothing (gradient estimator variance barely rises), while sampling beyond it degrades sharply, producing a knee whose location is predictable from a one-epoch correlation measurement and which shifts with architecture (larger receptive fields tolerate sparser sampling).
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes, training with losses computed on a random 25% of pixels will match full-loss training within 0.2 mIoU while 5% sampling loses at least 0.8 mIoU, the measured knee will match the gradient-field correlation length within a factor of 2, and a larger-receptive-field architecture will show its knee at proportionally sparser sampling. Kill the idea if accuracy degrades smoothly with no knee, or the knee location is uncorrelated with measured correlation length across architectures.
why_important: Loss computation and its backward pass on high-resolution outputs are a real compute cost; a validated redundancy law licenses principled subsampling and connects receptive-field geometry to supervision efficiency, a quantity relevant to any dense objective.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Pixel-sampled losses exist ad hoc; the correlation-length law with architecture-dependent knee prediction appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Sampling-rate ladders on two architectures with gradient-correlation measurement; locate knees; test the correlation-length predictor; verify with a third dataset at one rate.
main_risk: Rare-class pixels must be protected under sampling (stratified sampling), else the study measures class starvation rather than spatial redundancy.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Every labeled pixel is assumed to contribute usefully, and loss subsampling is expected to trade accuracy roughly linearly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Hard, informative pixels may be spatially isolated (boundary points), so uniform sampling might hit the knee far earlier than correlation length predicts, requiring importance-aware sampling to see the law.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 5 rates x 2 architectures x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: At fixed pixels-per-batch, spending the budget on more images with smaller crops beats fewer images with larger crops for gradient-noise reasons, except where context genuinely binds, giving a decomposable rule for the most common memory tradeoff in dense training.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense practitioners constantly trade image count against crop size under a fixed memory budget, guided by contradictory folklore (more images for BN vs bigger crops for context).
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Gradient estimator variance is dominated by between-image variation, so image count reduces noise roughly linearly while crop growth beyond the network's effective receptive field adds little signal; therefore the many-small configuration wins on optimization grounds, with exceptions confined to classes whose decisive evidence exceeds the crop size (large structures), producing a class-resolved crossover rather than a global winner.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] At matched pixels-per-batch and matched normalization (GN to remove BN confounds), 8-images-small-crops will beat 2-images-large-crops by at least 0.5 mIoU overall on Cityscapes, while the largest-object classes will show the reverse by at least 1.0 IoU, and measured gradient noise will be at least 1.5x lower for the many-small arm. Kill the idea if the many-small arm loses overall, or class-resolved effects show no size structure (context story fails everywhere).
why_important: This tradeoff is faced by every dense-training job that hits memory limits; a decomposed rule (default many-small, except large-evidence classes) with a noise measurement to arbitrate is directly actionable and clarifies which folklore applies when.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both folklores circulate; the matched-pixels controlled comparison with class-size decomposition under GN appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Matched-pixel arms {2x1024^2, 8x512^2, 32x256^2} under GN on Cityscapes and ADE20K; log gradient noise; report class-size-stratified accuracy over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Crop-size changes also shift boundary-pixel share and augmentation statistics; matching effective augmentation distributions across arms requires explicit design.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Bigger crops are generally worth the image-count sacrifice for dense tasks, per the context folklore.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Modern architectures with global attention may extract cross-crop-scale context so effectively that the large-crop arm wins broadly, not just on large classes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50-GN and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 3 arms x 2 architectures x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 4 days on one A100 40GB.

one_line_idea: Within-epoch presentation order leaves a measurable recency imprint on dense models at high learning rates: images seen late in the final epoch are predicted better than statistically identical images seen early, quantifying an ordering bias no one controls for.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Training data is reshuffled each epoch and the final model is treated as equally shaped by all training images; evaluation and dataset-design practice assume presentation order within an epoch is irrelevant.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Each step moves weights; at high LR the last portion of an epoch overwrites earlier micro-adaptations before any revisit, so a per-image benefit accrues to late positions, decaying with the LR at which the epoch was traversed; the effect concentrates on idiosyncratic image content (rare appearances) and vanishes as LR decays, making final-epoch order a small but systematic bias on per-image and per-rare-class results.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Randomizing final-epoch order across 8 replicas on Cityscapes at constant high LR, per-image validation-proxy loss (train-image held-out-crop loss) will correlate with within-epoch position at Spearman rho >= 0.15 for the last epoch (a small but consistent effect across replicas), the effect will shrink below rho = 0.05 at 10x lower final LR, and rare-appearance images will show 2x the positional effect of common ones. Kill the idea if positional correlation is indistinguishable from permutation-null at high LR, or shows no LR dependence.
why_important: A verified recency imprint quantifies one more unreported degree of freedom in training reproducibility, matters for benchmark comparisons that hinge on tenths of a point, and cleanly demonstrates the timescale on which dense models overwrite per-image adaptations.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ordering effects are studied for curricula at coarse scales; the within-final-epoch recency imprint on dense per-image outcomes appears unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train replicas differing only in final-epoch permutation; regress per-image proxy loss on position; repeat at two final LRs; stratify by image-content rarity (embedding density).
main_risk: Per-image outcome noise is large relative to the effect; the held-out-crop proxy and replica averaging are designed to reach adequate statistical power cheaply.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Within-epoch order is assumed fully neutralized by shuffling and averaging, with no per-image trace in the final model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: EMA or low final LRs in standard recipes may erase the imprint entirely, restricting the phenomenon to non-standard high-LR endings and limiting its practical scope.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 8 permutation replicas x 2 final-LR levels of a shared checkpoint's final epoch: about 1.5 days on one A100 (only final epochs differ; the shared prefix is trained once).

one_line_idea: Gradients from overlapping random crops of the same image are correlated almost linearly in their overlap area, so standard crop samplers waste batch slots; overlap-aware crop sampling recovers the wasted effective batch size for free.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Random-crop pipelines for dense training sample crops independently, sometimes drawing overlapping crops from the same image within or across nearby batches, and effective-batch-size accounting ignores this entirely.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Two crops sharing area produce gradient contributions whose correlation grows near-linearly with overlap fraction (shared receptive fields dominate), so expected effective sample count per batch is computable from the sampler's overlap distribution; a max-coverage/min-overlap sampler at identical cost raises effective batch size and should reproduce the accuracy of a measurably larger standard batch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measured pairwise gradient correlation will scale with crop overlap at r >= 0.8 linearity on Cityscapes, and an overlap-minimizing sampler will match the accuracy of standard sampling at 1.25x batch size within 0.15 mIoU while beating standard sampling at equal batch by at least 0.3 mIoU in the small-batch regime (4 images). Kill the idea if gradient correlation is weak (< 0.3 at 50% overlap) or the improved sampler yields under 0.1 mIoU at equal cost.
why_important: It quantifies a hidden inefficiency in the most ubiquitous dense-data pipeline component and delivers a drop-in sampler with predictable gains precisely where compute is scarcest (small-batch, high-resolution training).
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Crop sampling is treated as a solved preprocessing detail; the overlap-correlation law and effective-batch accounting appear unexamined.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure pairwise crop-gradient correlations as a function of overlap on frozen and training models; implement min-overlap sampling; run equal-cost and matched-effective-batch comparisons over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Per-crop gradient isolation requires micro-batching for measurement (cheap) and the sampler must preserve spatial coverage statistics to avoid trading overlap for coverage bias.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Crop randomness is assumed to deliver independent samples, with batch-size accounting done in image units.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Overlapping crops differ in augmentation (flip, color), which may decorrelate their gradients enough to make the waste negligible in practice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public): correlation measurement (hours) + 3 training arms x 3 seeds at 20k iterations: about 2 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Dense contrastive pretraining with within-image negatives learns positional shortcuts (discriminating by location rather than content), a failure mode absent with cross-image negatives, detectable by a position-decoding probe and fixable by position-debiased sampling.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Pixel/region contrastive methods draw negatives either within the same image or across images, a design choice made for implementation convenience with limited analysis of what each regime teaches.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Within-image negatives are separable by positional cues alone (feature maps carry position through padding and learned biases), so the objective can be satisfied by position-encoding rather than content-encoding features; this shortcut leaves a signature (high position-decoding accuracy from features, weak content transfer), grows with training length, and disappears when negatives come from other images where position is uninformative.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Features from within-image-negative pretraining will allow linear position decoding (patch coordinates) at least 2x above the cross-image-negative variant's accuracy, will trail it by at least 1.5 mIoU in downstream segmentation probes, and position-debiased within-image sampling (negatives matched on position distribution) will close at least 60% of the transfer gap. Kill the idea if position decodability does not differ between regimes, or debiasing closes under 20% of the gap (shortcut not the operative harm).
why_important: It identifies a concrete objective-design pathology in dense self-supervision with a cheap diagnostic and fix, and clarifies contradictory reports on within- vs cross-image contrastive designs by naming the variable that actually differs.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Positional shortcuts are known in other SSL contexts (padding artifacts); the within-image-negative pathway, its growth dynamics, and the debiased-sampling fix for dense contrastive learning appear new. Distinct from occupied W13-P1-E-075 (patch-assignment boundary ill-posedness in patch-supervised models): this concerns negative-sampling geometry, not boundary assignment.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Pretrain matched models with within-image, cross-image, and position-debiased within-image negatives; probe position decodability over training; evaluate downstream probes over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Position decodability exists even in supervised features; the comparison is differential (between regimes), which the matched-training design supports.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Negative-source choice is treated as an efficiency detail, with within-image negatives considered a valid dense-friendly default.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Position information may be a useful feature (dense tasks need it), so the shortcut may be benign or even beneficial, showing up as no downstream gap despite decodability differences.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ResNet-50 dense-contrastive pretraining (public implementations) on Pascal VOC images (public) at reduced scale, 3 regimes x 2 seeds x 100 epochs + probes: about 3 days on one RTX 4090.

one_line_idea: The gradient noise scale of dense training drifts by an order of magnitude within a single run (unlike classification's comparative stability), so any fixed batch size is wrong for most of the run and a noise-tracking batch-size ramp captures measurable gains.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Gradient-noise-scale reasoning is used to pick batch sizes once per task, assuming the appropriate batch size is roughly constant over a run; dense training inherits this assumption from classification practice.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Dense tasks concentrate late-phase learning in small pixel populations (boundaries, rare classes), collapsing the effective sample count per batch as interiors saturate; the gradient noise scale therefore rises steeply within-run, meaning early training is over-batched (wasted parallelism) and late training under-batched (noise-limited), and a batch ramp tracking measured noise achieves better accuracy-per-FLOP than any fixed batch.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Measured gradient noise scale will rise by at least 5x from the first to last training decile on Cityscapes and COCO (versus under 2x for matched classification), and a two-stage batch ramp (small-to-large tracking the measurement) will match fixed-large-batch accuracy at no more than 70% of its total FLOPs, or beat fixed-small-batch by at least 0.5 mIoU/AP at equal FLOPs. Kill the idea if within-run noise drift is under 2x (no dense-specific structure) or the ramp fails to beat both fixed baselines on the accuracy-compute frontier.
why_important: Batch-size folklore transplanted from classification misallocates dense-training compute at both ends of the run; a within-run law with a simple ramp policy improves the accuracy-compute frontier using measurements any pipeline can log.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Gradient-noise-scale batch selection is established methodology; its within-run drift structure for dense tasks and the tracking-ramp consequence appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument noise-scale measurement through full runs on segmentation, detection, and matched classification; implement a two-stage ramp from the measured curve; compare accuracy-FLOP frontiers over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Batch changes interact with LR schedules; the ramp arms must apply established batch-LR co-scaling to avoid conflating a badly-scaled LR with the batching claim.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] One well-chosen batch size serves a whole run, with within-run adaptation considered needless complexity.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Late-phase noise growth may coincide with such small gradient magnitudes that extra batch parallelism buys nothing practical, flattening the frontier difference below measurability.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 on Cityscapes and RetinaNet-R50 on COCO (public), instrumented runs + 3 batching policies x 2 seeds at short schedules: about 4 days on one A100 (large-batch phases use gradient accumulation with GN to stay single-GPU-honest).

one_line_idea: Photometric augmentation strength and learning rate are partially interchangeable noise sources in dense training, with iso-accuracy contours revealing a measurable exchange rate, so recipes tuned at one LR silently mis-tune augmentation at another.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Augmentation strength and LR are tuned as independent hyperparameters in dense recipes, and transferred independently when schedules change.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Label-preserving photometric augmentation perturbs gradients much like extra minibatch noise; since SGD's implicit regularization depends on total noise level, augmentation strength and LR trade off along iso-accuracy contours in the (LR, aug-strength) plane with a quantifiable negative-slope exchange band, until augmentation begins destroying task-relevant information and the contours collapse.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On a 5x5 (LR x photometric-strength) grid on Cityscapes, the top-accuracy region will form a negatively sloped band (higher LR pairing with weaker augmentation) with contour slope stable across two architectures within a factor of 2, and total-gradient-noise measurements will be approximately constant along iso-accuracy contours (within 30%). Kill the idea if the accuracy surface is separable (optimal augmentation independent of LR, interaction below noise) or noise is non-constant along contours by 3x+.
why_important: An exchange-rate law explains why augmentation recipes break when schedules change, enables porting recipes across LR regimes by noise matching, and grounds the augmentation-as-regularization intuition in a measured optimization quantity for dense tasks.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Augmentation-LR interactions are folk-suspected; the iso-contour exchange-rate quantification with noise accounting on dense tasks appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train the 5x5 grid on two architectures with gradient-noise logging; map accuracy surfaces; test contour slope stability and noise constancy along contours.
main_risk: Photometric strength is multidimensional; a single pre-registered strength scalar (composed jitter magnitudes) keeps the grid tractable at the cost of generality.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Augmentation tunes invariances and LR tunes optimization, so their optima are treated as independent.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Augmentation noise is structured (correlated within images) unlike minibatch noise, so its regularization may be qualitatively different and refuse to trade against LR along any stable contour.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 25 cells x 2 architectures at 20k iterations, 1 seed with corner replication: about 5 days on one A100; the single-architecture grid (2.5 days) tests the core claim.
