one_line_idea: Channel dropout and spatially structured dropout in dense decoders trade places as decoder width changes, because their effective noise targets (feature redundancy vs spatial redundancy) scale oppositely with width, predicting a width-conditioned reversal that folklore misses.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense heads use dropout variants (channel/2D-structured) inherited from classification or chosen by anecdote, with inconsistent reported benefits across architectures.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Channel dropout regularizes against inter-channel co-adaptation, which grows with decoder width, while spatial dropout regularizes against local spatial co-adaptation, which is width-independent; therefore narrow decoders benefit more from spatial variants (channel dropout destroys scarce capacity) and wide decoders from channel variants, producing a systematic ranking reversal at a measurable width threshold.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across decoder widths {64, 128, 256, 512} on Cityscapes, the channel-vs-spatial dropout accuracy ranking will reverse exactly once, with the reversal width consistent across two backbone families within one grid step, and channel-redundancy measurements (feature correlation spectra) will track the crossover. Kill the idea if one variant dominates at all widths in both families, or the reversal point is family-inconsistent by 2+ steps.
why_important: It converts an arbitrary regularizer choice into a width-conditioned rule with a measurable driver, and illustrates how regularizer folklore fails to transfer because it silently conditions on architecture scale.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Dropout-variant comparisons exist per architecture; the width-conditioned reversal law with redundancy tracking appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Grid width x {channel, spatial, none} on two backbones; measure channel-correlation spectra per width; locate ranking reversals over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Dropout rates must be tuned per cell (fixed rates would confound rate mis-tuning with variant choice), tripling the sweep but keeping the comparison honest.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] One dropout variant is assumed generically better for dense heads, with width treated as irrelevant to the choice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Normalization layers may neutralize both dropout variants at all practical widths, making the entire comparison moot in modern dense heads (also a publishable audit outcome).
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ with R50 and MobileNetV3 backbones (public) on Cityscapes (public), 4 widths x 3 variants x small rate sweep at 20k iterations: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Stochastic depth in ViT dense fine-tuning is an implicit layer-wise LR decay in disguise (deeper blocks receive fewer effective updates), so its tuned drop-rate profile should be reproducible by an explicit LLRD profile matched to expected update rates, unifying two rituals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Stochastic depth (randomly skipping residual blocks) is tuned for ViT fine-tuning alongside layer-wise LR decay, treated as an independent regularizer with its own sweep.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Skipping a block removes its update that step, so a linearly increasing drop-rate profile multiplies each block's expected update count by its keep probability, exactly what LLRD does deterministically; if the regularization-relevant variable is per-block effective update budget, then LLRD matched to the keep-probability profile reproduces stochastic depth's accuracy, and their combination is redundant (no additive gain).
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Update-rate-matched LLRD will come within 0.3 mIoU of tuned stochastic depth on ADE20K ViT fine-tuning, and adding stochastic depth on top of matched LLRD will improve by under 0.2 mIoU (redundancy), while a noise-component control (stochastic depth with compensated LR to equalize expected updates) will isolate any residual stochasticity benefit above 0.3 mIoU if it exists. Kill the idea if matched LLRD trails by more than 0.8 mIoU (the stochasticity itself, not the update budget, carries the effect).
why_important: Two separately swept knobs collapsing into one variable halves a common tuning burden and clarifies whether the skip-noise in stochastic depth does anything beyond budget shaping for dense fine-tuning, a mechanism question with consequences for efficient-training design.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Both techniques are standard; the update-budget equivalence test with a compensated-noise control appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {tuned stochastic depth, matched LLRD, both, LR-compensated stochastic depth, neither} on ViT-B ADE20K fine-tuning over 2 seeds; compare accuracy and per-block update statistics.
main_risk: Stochastic depth also changes forward-pass statistics (shallower effective network per step), a channel LLRD lacks; the compensated control partially isolates it but normalization interactions may blur attribution.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stochastic depth is understood as a distinct stochastic regularizer whose benefits are additive with LLRD.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The ensemble-of-depths interpretation may be the real mechanism (function-space averaging), which no deterministic LR profile reproduces, sending the equivalence test to its kill branch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: ViT-B MAE or DINOv2 (public) with UperNet on ADE20K (public), 5 arms x 2 seeds at 80k iterations: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Label smoothing in segmentation trades boundary representation quality for interior stability: it collapses the logit structure that encodes soft class transitions at boundaries, predicting opposite effects on interior and boundary metrics that aggregate mIoU conceals.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Label smoothing is applied to dense classification heads as a default-ish regularizer with modest aggregate effects; classification studies show it collapses within-class logit structure.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] At true class transitions, unsmoothed training lets logits encode graded mixtures (an honest representation of boundary pixels); smoothing forces all pixels toward the same target geometry, erasing the graded structure and pushing boundary decisions toward hard, spatially unstable transitions, so boundary-band accuracy and transition-zone logit entropy structure degrade while interior accuracy mildly improves from the regularization.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] On Cityscapes with smoothing 0.1 vs none, interior accuracy will improve by 0.2-0.6 points while 4px-trimap boundary F-score drops by at least 0.8 points, and the spatial profile of logit entropy across boundaries will flatten by at least 40% under smoothing; masking smoothing off within boundary bands will retain the interior gain while removing at least 60% of the boundary tax. Kill the idea if boundary metrics do not degrade (< 0.3) or the band-masked variant fails to decouple the effects.
why_important: A metric-dependent sign flip hidden in a default regularizer matters for every boundary-sensitive application, and the band-masked variant is an immediately usable fix; the result also documents that dense logit geometry carries task-relevant structure that classification-derived regularizers destroy.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Label smoothing's logit-collapse effect is documented for classification; its spatially heterogeneous consequences for dense boundaries and the band-masked remedy appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {none, global smoothing, band-masked smoothing} on two segmentation setups; measure region-decomposed accuracy and cross-boundary logit-entropy profiles over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Boundary effects may be small relative to seed noise at standard scales; 3 seeds and paired-image analysis are budgeted to resolve 0.8-point effects.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Label smoothing is a benign or mildly positive default for dense heads, evaluated on aggregate metrics only.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Graded boundary logits may reflect ambiguity the model should not encode anyway, and smoothing's stabilization could actually improve boundary placement consistency, reversing the predicted sign.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 and SegFormer-B0 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 3 arms x 2 architectures x 3 seeds at 40k iterations: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: The ramp-up period folklore for auxiliary regularizer weights exists to protect training until the supervised gradient stabilizes, so an adaptive ramp triggered by measured gradient-norm stabilization should match hand-tuned ramps across setups with zero tuning.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Auxiliary objective weights (consistency terms, feature regularizers) in dense training use hand-tuned linear or sigmoid ramp-ups over a tuned number of steps, re-tuned per dataset and schedule.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The ramp's function is to keep auxiliary pressure weak while the supervised gradient field is still large and rapidly rotating (early chaos), and to reach full strength once supervised dynamics stabilize; the correct ramp clock is therefore the measured stabilization of supervised gradient statistics (norm and direction change rate), not step count, so an adaptive ramp keyed to that signal transfers across datasets, budgets, and LR schedules without re-tuning.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] The adaptive ramp with one universal threshold will come within 0.3 mIoU of the best hand-tuned ramp on 4 dense semi-supervised/regularized setups spanning two datasets and two budgets, while transplanted fixed ramps (tuned on one setup, moved to another) will lose at least 0.8 mIoU somewhere. Kill the idea if the adaptive rule needs per-setup thresholds to reach parity, or fixed ramps transfer fine everywhere (nothing to fix).
why_important: Ramp lengths are pure tuning burden with no accepted meaning; deriving them from an observable training state removes a hyperparameter and validates a general principle for scheduling any auxiliary pressure against main-task dynamics.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Ramp-ups are classic; the gradient-stabilization clock and its transfer claim appear untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On 4 setups, grid fixed ramps to find local optima; run the adaptive rule with a single threshold; run transplanted-ramp arms; compare over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Defining stabilization (windowed direction-change rate below threshold) has freedom; pre-registering the statistic and threshold from a pilot setup avoids adaptive-rule overfitting.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Ramp lengths are arbitrary schedule constants to be tuned, with step count as the natural clock.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ramp requirements may track the auxiliary term's own dynamics (e.g., teacher quality in consistency setups) rather than supervised stabilization, breaking the single-clock rule.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 semi-supervised (public protocols) on Cityscapes and Pascal VOC (public), 4 setups x {3 fixed ramps, adaptive, transplanted} x 2 seeds at short schedules: about 4.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Wide random-resize ranges pay their cost only early: scale-range annealing (wide early, narrow late) should match full wide-range training on scale robustness while recovering the late-phase accuracy that wide ranges tax, resolving the scale-augmentation dilemma as a scheduling problem.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Random resize/scale augmentation ranges for dense training trade in-range robustness against convergence quality, and the range is fixed for the whole run by convention.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Scale diversity teaches scale-robust features, a structural property acquired early and retained; late in training, wide scale jitter mostly injects gradient variance that impedes fine consolidation without adding robustness, so annealing the range concentrates diversity where it builds structure and calm where consolidation needs it, dominating any fixed range on the joint (robustness, accuracy) frontier.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Scale-annealed training on Cityscapes will match wide-fixed training's multi-scale evaluation robustness within 0.3 mIoU (across 0.5x-2x test scales) while beating it at native scale by at least 0.6 mIoU, and will beat narrow-fixed training's multi-scale robustness by at least 1.5 mIoU; scale-robustness probes will confirm the property is acquired in the first half and retained after annealing. Kill the idea if annealed training loses more than 0.5 mIoU of multi-scale robustness (the property decays without continued exposure) or shows no native-scale gain over wide-fixed.
why_important: It converts a static tradeoff into a free-lunch schedule if retention holds, and measures the retention question itself (are augmentation-taught invariances stable once acquired?), which matters for every invariance-oriented augmentation in dense pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Progressive/annealed augmentation appears in efficiency recipes; the retention-based account with joint frontier measurement for scale specifically appears untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Arms {narrow, wide, annealed wide-to-narrow, reverse-annealed} on Cityscapes and ADE20K; evaluate native and multi-scale accuracy; probe scale robustness at checkpoints to time acquisition and test retention.
main_risk: Multi-scale evaluation protocol choices (which scales, interpolation) shape the robustness measurement; pre-registering the protocol prevents post-hoc metric selection.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] The augmentation distribution must match the desired invariance throughout training, implying wide ranges must persist to the end.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scale robustness may decay measurably once wide jitter stops (invariance needs maintenance), in which case the reverse-annealed arm and retention probes will document maintenance requirements instead.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes + ADE20K (public), 4 arms x 2 datasets x 2 seeds at 40k iterations with multi-scale evaluation: about 4 days on one A100.

why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Decay-augmentation interactions are folk-observed in recipes; the substitution-band quantification with channel-population overlap measurement for dense tasks appears new.

core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Photometric transforms leave the spatial supervision structure intact (same pixels, same geometry), acting as label-preserving gradient noise; geometric transforms re-map the correspondence between network equivariance structure and supervision, decorrelating per-pixel gradients across views and specifically training spatial-equivariance pathways; consequently, matched-strength substitutions will fail asymmetrically: geometric-for-photometric substitution preserves noise benefits but photometric-for-geometric cannot restore equivariance training, showing up as task-dependent irreplaceability (geometry-heavy tasks like depth suffer more from losing geometric augmentation).

one_line_idea: Loss spikes in dense training are triggered by reproducible image-crop-augmentation conjunctions, not random batch bad luck: the same content configurations spike across seeds, making spike-trigger mining a dataset diagnostic rather than a stability mystery.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense training runs exhibit occasional loss spikes that practitioners attribute to unlucky batches and handle generically with clipping or LR reduction, without asking whether spikes have stable causes.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Spikes arise when specific content meets specific transformation states (extreme crops of unusual structures, augmentation pushing inputs outside learned statistics); these conjunctions are properties of the data-augmentation distribution, not of the stochastic trajectory, so spike triggers replicate across seeds and identify a stable pathological subdistribution whose characterization explains what the model cannot yet absorb at each phase.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Logging per-step spike events (batch loss above 5x running median) across 4 seeds on Cityscapes and COCO training, the top-decile spike-triggering (image, crop-region, augmentation-bin) conjunctions will overlap across seeds with Jaccard >= 0.4 (versus < 0.05 for permutation null), and re-presenting mined triggers to an independently seeded run will reproduce elevated loss (>= 3x median) in at least 60% of cases. Kill the idea if cross-seed trigger overlap is below 0.1 or re-presentation reproduces spikes in under 20% of cases (spikes are trajectory-idiosyncratic after all).
why_important: If spikes are data-conditioned and reproducible, stability engineering gains a diagnostic target (characterize and handle the trigger subdistribution) instead of blanket interventions, and the trigger catalog itself documents which content-transformation regions of the input space remain unabsorbed during training.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spike studies in large-model training focus on optimizer state; the cross-seed trigger-reproducibility question for dense vision appears unasked.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument spike logging with full batch provenance across seeds; compute cross-seed trigger overlap against permutation nulls; run re-presentation probes on a held-out seed.
main_risk: Spike definitions and provenance binning involve choices; pre-registering the threshold (5x median) and binning scheme prevents diagnostic tuning.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Loss spikes are treated as stochastic accidents of batching, worth suppressing but not explaining.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Spikes may be dominated by optimizer-state resonances (moment estimates entering bad regimes) that content merely modulates, in which case re-presentation without the matching optimizer state will fail to reproduce them.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 on Cityscapes and RetinaNet-R50 on COCO (public), 4 seeds x short schedules with provenance logging + re-presentation probes: about 4 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Backbone parameters in dense training sit at the edge of stability (top curvature hovering near the 2/LR boundary) like classification networks do, but dense decoder heads systematically do not, revealing a two-regime landscape that schedule design currently ignores.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Edge-of-stability behavior (top Hessian eigenvalue equilibrating near 2/LR under gradient descent) is documented for classification training; whether dense architectures' heterogeneous components share one stability regime is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The per-pixel averaged loss gives decoder heads much smaller and spatially diffuse curvature contributions, while shared backbones accumulate curvature from all pixels; module-resolved curvature tracking will show backbones at the stability edge (curvature rides the 2/LR line) while decoders sit far below it, implying decoders are effectively under-stepped at the global LR and could absorb larger module-wise steps, a structural inefficiency in every single-LR dense recipe.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Module-resolved top-curvature estimates during Cityscapes training will show backbone curvature within a factor of 2 of the 2/LR boundary for most of training while decoder-head curvature stays at least 5x below it, and raising decoder LR by the measured slack factor will improve final mIoU by at least 0.4 without instability. Kill the idea if decoder curvature also rides the edge (within 2x), or exploiting the slack yields under 0.15 mIoU (slack real but worthless).
why_important: It extends a central empirical law of neural training to structured architectures, identifies which module actually constrains the LR, and converts the finding into a measurable module-LR assignment rule beyond the folklore 10x head multiplier.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Edge-of-stability studies use monolithic networks on classification; module-resolved analysis on dense architectures with an exploitation test appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Track module-wise top curvature via power iteration on module-restricted Hessian-vector products during training; verify regime split; run decoder-LR-raised arms at the measured slack over 2 seeds.
main_risk: Hessian-vector products on full dense models are costly; restricting to periodic measurements (every 500 steps) and subsampled batches keeps overhead under 20%.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stability is treated as a global property of the run, with one LR bounded by one worst-case curvature.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Adam's preconditioning changes the relevant stability criterion per parameter, potentially equalizing effective edges across modules and dissolving the two-regime picture.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public) with SGD, instrumented run + 2 exploitation arms x 2 seeds at 40k iterations: about 2.5 days on one A100.

one_line_idea: Divergence events in ViT dense fine-tuning are preceded by attention-entropy collapse in a small identifiable set of heads, providing an early-warning signal several hundred steps ahead of the loss explosion and a targeted intervention (per-head temperature) that prevents it.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Transformer training exhibits attention-entropy collapse associated with instability, documented mainly for classification and language pretraining; dense fine-tuning divergences are handled reactively (restart with lower LR) without early-warning instrumentation.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] In dense fine-tuning, divergence is seeded when particular heads (typically high-resolution, late-block heads processing boundary-dense tokens) sharpen toward near-deterministic attention; the entropy collapse of those heads precedes global loss explosion by a detectable margin, and clamping only the collapsing heads' attention temperature interrupts the cascade at negligible accuracy cost, establishing causality rather than correlation.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 20 deliberately high-LR ViT dense fine-tunes, at least 70% of divergences will show >= 50% entropy drop in under 5% of heads at least 200 steps before the loss exceeds 10x its running median, per-head clamping triggered by the entropy signal will prevent at least 60% of divergences without losing more than 0.3 mIoU relative to stable-LR baselines, and randomly-targeted clamping will prevent under 20%. Kill the idea if collapses precede divergence in under 30% of cases (signal unreliable) or targeted clamping performs no better than random targeting (no causal role).
why_important: It upgrades a documented correlation into an early-warning-plus-intervention protocol for dense fine-tuning, where divergences waste substantial compute, and localizes which attention computations are fragile under dense supervision.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Entropy collapse is documented as an instability correlate in transformer pretraining; the head-localized early-warning timing and targeted-intervention causality test in dense fine-tuning appear new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Provoke divergences with an aggressive-LR grid; log per-head entropy trajectories; measure lead times; run signal-triggered targeted vs random clamping arms.
main_risk: Provoked divergences may differ mechanistically from in-the-wild ones at standard LR; a smaller observational arm at recipe LRs checks the signature's ecological validity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Divergence is treated as a global LR problem to be avoided by conservative schedules, not as a localized, interceptable cascade.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Entropy collapse may be a symptom appearing after the true trigger (optimizer-state blowup), making lead times too short or interventions ineffective despite the correlation.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B2 and ViT-S+UperNet (public) on ADE20K (public), 20 short high-LR runs + intervention arms: about 4 days on one A100 (divergent runs terminate early, capping cost).

one_line_idea: Dense fine-tuning divergence obeys a universal boundary in the head-to-backbone update-ratio: across tasks and architectures, runs diverge when the sustained ratio exceeds a shared threshold, yielding a one-number stability criterion and a ratio-capping guard that replaces conservative global LR reduction.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] Dense fine-tuning stability is managed by global LR caution, warmup, and folklore multipliers, with each failure handled by rerunning at lower LR; no quantitative cross-setup stability criterion exists.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] The destabilizing interaction is the head rewriting the feature-consumer relationship faster than the backbone can co-adapt; this is captured by the sustained ratio of head update magnitude to backbone update magnitude (in normalized per-parameter units), and divergence occurs when the ratio exceeds a threshold that is approximately shared across tasks and architectures because it reflects the generic co-adaptation bandwidth of gradient descent, not task specifics.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Across 30 runs spanning segmentation, depth, and detection fine-tunes with varied LRs and multipliers, diverging and stable runs will be separable by a sustained update-ratio threshold with at least 85% classification accuracy, the fitted thresholds per task family will agree within a factor of 3, and a ratio-capping controller (scaling head LR down when the ratio approaches the boundary) will train stably at base LRs 2x above the uncapped divergence point with final accuracy within 0.3 of the best stable baseline. Kill the idea if no ratio threshold separates outcomes above 65% accuracy, or per-task thresholds disagree by more than 10x (no universality).
why_important: A validated universal criterion turns stability from trial-and-error into a monitored invariant, enables more aggressive base LRs (faster fine-tuning) behind a cheap guard, and identifies interface co-adaptation as the binding constraint in dense transfer stability.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Update-ratio heuristics exist informally in optimizer lore; a cross-task universality test with a capping controller for dense fine-tuning appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate the 30-run outcome dataset with ratio logging; fit and cross-validate the threshold across task families; implement the capping controller and test at aggressive base LRs.
main_risk: Divergence labels need a consistent definition (loss exceeding 10x median for 100+ steps without recovery); borderline oscillating runs must be pre-classified by rule.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] Stability limits are task- and architecture-specific, requiring per-setup LR discovery with no transferable quantitative criterion.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Divergences may have multiple mechanistic families (interface shock, curvature blowup, precision events) with different signatures, capping any single-criterion classifier well below the pre-registered bar.
fastest_falsification_experiment: SegFormer-B0/ADE20K, DPT/NYUv2, RetinaNet/COCO-minitrain (all public), 30 short runs + 6 controller runs: about 4.5 days on one A100 (diverging runs terminate early).

one_line_idea: Recovery from training spikes is spatially unequal: interior and frequent-class accuracy heals within hundreds of steps while rare-class and boundary accuracy exhibits hysteresis lasting many epochs, so a run's spike history taxes exactly the metrics that aggregate curves hide.
problem: [KNOWN FACT] After loss spikes, training curves visibly recover and practitioners treat the incident as closed once aggregate loss returns to trend; whether recovery is uniform across the structured output is unexamined.
core_hypothesis: [HYPOTHESIS] Spikes disproportionately corrupt low-redundancy knowledge (rare-class prototypes, fine boundary placements) whose gradient signal is too sparse to rebuild quickly, while high-redundancy knowledge (frequent-class interiors) re-converges almost immediately; therefore post-spike deficits persist selectively, spike-heavy runs end measurably worse on rare/boundary metrics at matched final aggregate loss, and a short post-spike replay of rare-class-dense content erases the selective deficit.
falsifiable_prediction: [EXPECTED RESULT] Injecting controlled spikes (temporary 10x LR for 20 steps) at three points in Cityscapes training, frequent-class interior accuracy will recover to control-trajectory levels within 500 steps while the rarest-quintile class IoU remains at least 1.0 below control for 5000+ steps, spike-injected runs will end at least 0.8 IoU behind controls on rare classes despite matching mean loss within 1%, and targeted replay after spikes will close at least 60% of the persistent gap. Kill the idea if recovery timescales differ by less than 2x across populations or final rare-class deficits are under 0.3 IoU.
why_important: It shows that stability incidents leave class-selective scars invisible to the curves everyone monitors, justifying spike-history reporting and targeted-replay remediation, and quantifies knowledge redundancy as the variable governing what training forgets under perturbation.
why_possibly_novel: [MODEL SPECULATION / unverified] Spike recovery is assessed on aggregate losses in practice; population-resolved hysteresis measurement with a remediation arm appears new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Controlled spike injection at pre-registered points vs twin controls; population-resolved accuracy tracking at high checkpoint frequency; targeted-replay remediation arms over 3 seeds.
main_risk: Injected spikes must approximate natural ones; a small observational validation on naturally spiking runs (from the trigger-mining study design) checks the injection's ecological validity.
community_default_belief: [MODEL SPECULATION] A recovered loss curve means a recovered model; spike incidents are not tracked as run metadata anywhere.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimizer state (Adam second moments) may buffer rare-class parameters against spikes precisely because their gradients are sparse, inverting the predicted vulnerability ordering.
fastest_falsification_experiment: DeepLabv3+ R50 (public) on Cityscapes (public), 3 injection points x {spike, control, spike+replay} x 3 seeds at 40k iterations: about 3.5 days on one A100.
